Regarding the statement that "original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) follows defilement and undergoes discrimination," it means that the essence of original awakening is fundamentally free from thought and likewise devoid of characteristics;
it is only because of non-awakening (*a-bodha*) that thoughts and characteristics arise adventitiously. Thus, based upon non-awakening, initial awakening arises, whereby one is finally able to...
The awakened mind is free from thought, revealing the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*). By overturning defilement, it becomes pure, giving rise to the aspect of pure wisdom.
Because it relies upon this aspect of wisdom, there is the aspect of inconceivable activity according to the perceptions of sentient beings;

thus it is said that "following defiled discrimination, two kinds of aspects arise. Regarding these two aspects: in terms of their functional activity (*karmopayoga*), the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are not separate from the *dharmakāya*. In terms of wisdom...
As for the marks, these are the marks of virtue that do not depart from the essence of awakening; therefore, it is said that they are not separated from that original awakening (*mūla-awakening*).

Regarding the phrase "How so? below, this interrogates and enumerates the two marks. As for what is called the "mark of the purity of wisdom," it refers to the internal permeation based on the principle of the dharma of original awakening.
The external perfuming of the True Suchness (tathatā) teachings leads one to receive that auditory perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*), thereby augmenting the power of innate understanding.

Because one realizes that the essence of cognition is inherently free from conceptual thought and that its self-nature is originally pure, one subsequently cultivates the practice of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) without external objects, thereby distancing oneself from prior sensory domains.

This constitutes the stage prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) where one practices perfuming in reliance upon the teachings; hence it is said: "perfuming by the power of relying on the Dharma. Through this perfuming...

Through cultivation, one attains knowledge in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because there is no prior objective realm and because of this knowledge in accordance with reality, one immediately accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and extensively cultivates all practices;
hence it is called "practice in accordance with reality. This refers to the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Upon reaching the fulfillment of skillful means (*upāya*), one then destroys the aspect of non-awakening within the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*), manifests the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and extinguishes karma.
The characteristic of the continuous succession of the evolving [consciousnesses] is that the nature of wisdom (jñāna) is pure; this is called the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom.

This is because, during the state of delusion, the two dharmas of awakening and non-awakening are conjoined, whereby the evolving consciousnesses, the ālayavijñāna, and their objective supports arise in mutual dependence without interruption.
Now, by means of the power of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), one destroys the marks of non-awakening (*a-bodhi*) and reveals the Dharma-body of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
There is only the nature of original awakening and no marks of non-awakening; therefore, it is said that the marks of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃyukta-vijñāna*) are destroyed.

The six defiled marks, such as the transformation of karma, are extinguished. When the nature of wisdom is pure and serene, there are no marks of dependence or interruption; hence, it is said that they are "extinguished."
This refers to the characteristic of the continuous mind.
What is the meaning of this? All characteristics of consciousness are ignorance; yet the characteristic of ignorance does not depart from the nature of awakening.
It is neither destructible nor indestructible, like the water of the great ocean which moves due to the wind, though the nature of the water remains as it is.

The characteristic of wind and [the characteristic of water] are not separate from one another; yet, water does not possess the nature of motion. If the wind ceases, the characteristic of motion ceases, but the moist nature is not destroyed.
In this same way, the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings is moved by the wind of ignorance.
Mind and ignorance are both without form and are not separate from one another; yet, the mind does not possess the nature of motion. If ignorance ceases, [the characteristic of motion ceases].

"Continuation then ceases. Because the nature of wisdom is indestructible, this interrogative explanation clarifies the meaning of the characteristic of cessation as manifesting the nature; it demonstrates that while characteristics may perish, the nature does not.
The first phrase raises the preceding point, asking: "What is the meaning of this characteristic of cessation manifesting the nature? [The text continues with] "Because all... and so forth.
This explains and establishes the preceding meaning: "Mind" refers to the continuous mind, which is the sixfold defiled consciousness;

"consciousness" refers to the synthetic consciousness, which is the *ālaya-vijñāna*. These characteristics of the deluded movement of mind and consciousness are all formed based upon non-enlightenment (*a-prabodha*).
Therefore, all these are ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, they all arise through the transformation of that pure mind; thus, they are not separate from the nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
Consequently, one knows that consciousness is composed of the two factors of awakening and non-awakening.

As for the statement that it is "neither destructible nor indestructible," this is because the characteristics of the deluded movement of consciousness are entirely ignorance; therefore, it is not indestructible.
[The text] is destroyed. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "It breaks the characteristics of the harmonious consciousness and extinguishes the characteristics of the continuous mind.

Because mind and consciousness do not depart from the awakened nature (*bodhi*), they cannot be destroyed; rather, it is their *characteristics* (*lakṣaṇa*) that can be destroyed while their *nature* (*svabhāva*) cannot.

Thus, when the characteristics of mind and consciousness are extinguished, the pure wisdom of the Dharma-body manifests. As in the section beginning with "Like the great ocean," [the text] provides an illustration.

This is a further illustration by way of analogy. The passage beginning with "In this way, sentient beings... explains the point through the application of dharmas. Water is a metaphor for the pure mind; wind is a metaphor for ignorance;
and the movement of the waves is a metaphor for the continuity of karma and so forth. Thus, wind and water are inseparable and can produce the appearance of waves.
Nevertheless, because the nature of water is immovable, when the wind ceases the waves become still, yet the moist nature remains unimpaired. This serves as an analogy for the mind.
Although the union of these two factors— ignorance and [the mind]— is able to produce the characteristics of the evolution of karma and so forth, because the nature of the mind is immovable,
delusion ceases and movement perishes, while the nature of wisdom remains undestroyed.

Regarding the characteristic of inconceivable activity: by relying on the characteristic of pure wisdom, it is able to produce all supreme and wondrous objects—namely, the characteristics of immeasurable merit—which are eternally uninterrupted.
In accordance with the faculties of sentient beings, they manifest in various ways through spontaneous correspondence, thereby bringing about benefit.
This passage cites and explains the characteristics of the inconceivable karmic activity. Regarding what is called the "characteristics of inconceivable karmic activity":

it refers to how all bodhisattvas, relying on the characteristics of the Buddha’s wisdom, perceive their own physical forms, marks, and signs of excellence, as well as their environments and adornments, each of which is immeasurable.

Therefore, it is said that based on the characteristic of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*), one is able to produce all supreme and wondrous objects; this is what the capacity itself creates.

Now, these supreme and wondrous objects refer to what is called the body having immeasurable colors, and those colors having immeasurable marks, even extending to the dwelling-place and the fruit of reliance, which likewise possess immeasurable varieties of adornments. According to what is appropriate, they are always able to [manifest].
Abiding and maintaining, neither destroying nor losing, it is said that the marks of immeasurable merit are eternally uninterrupted. Yet, within ultimate function, there is non-action;
though the marks of wisdom are markless, they do not hinder beings from receiving benefit according to their faculties, manifesting marks in accordance with their capacities.
It cannot be conceived through the duality of existence and non-existence; therefore, it is called the "inconceivable characteristic of activity.
Furthermore, as for the characteristic of the essence of awakening, there are four kinds of great meanings that are equal to empty space, like a pure mirror.
This citation uses a metaphor to further clarify the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the essence of awakening (*bodhi*). Regarding the phrase "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*):

it means that while the four characteristics of the essence of awakening have already been fully analyzed previously, they are now elucidated once more; hence, the term "Furthermore. Regarding the phrase "There are four kinds of great meanings," etc.:

it means that because the essence of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) possesses the fourfold meanings of being devoid of characteristics, manifesting characteristics, and illuminating objects with brilliant clarity, it is used as a metaphor.
Like a pure mirror, each and every aspect of its meaning pervades the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said to be "equal to empty space.

Thus, empty space serves as the metaphor for the meaning of "greatness," while the mirror serves as the metaphor for the four aspects. Now, these two metaphors are presented together because if only the metaphor of empty space were used, the four meanings would not be revealed;
and if only the metaphor of the mirror were used, the meaning of greatness would not be revealed. Therefore, they are presented in tandem.

These two metaphors merely serve to mutually elucidate one another. However, within the subsequent section on the four mirrors, while the four meanings are clearly revealed, the meaning of "pervasiveness" is not explicitly manifest.
Although it is not stated in the text, its meaning is nonetheless complete. Regarding the metaphor of the mirror for the four characteristics: first is the empty mirror.
This refers to: first, being free from all marks (*sarva-nimitta-vigata*); second, the non-empty mirror, whose substance is not non-existent and which can manifest myriad images;
third, the pure mirror, meaning it has been polished and freed from defilement; and fourth, the mirror for enjoyment, which is placed upon a high stand so that those in need may utilize it.

Furthermore, the former two refer to natural purity (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*) as spoken of during the stage when the cause is latent; the latter two refer to purity through the removal of defilements (*vaimalya-vyavadāna*) as spoken of at the time of the manifestation of the fruit.
It is so explained.
What are the four? First is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is. It is far removed from all marks of mental objects;
no phenomena can appear within it, for it does not possess the quality of cognitive illumination.

This provides a general inquiry and a specific explanation regarding the "mirror of emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnya-ādarśa*). Regarding the phrase "the mirror of emptiness as it truly is":

this refers to the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), wherein the characteristics of subject and object are absent, and no phenomena can manifest. It is like a clear mirror in which no images originally exist, nor can anything be manifested.
Therefore, it is called the "mirror of emptiness as it truly is. As for the phrase "because it does not have the sense of cognitive illumination," this concludes the explanation of "as it truly is."
The meaning of emptiness refers to the mirror of emptiness as it truly is; this is the sense of empty quiescence, not the sense of cognitive illumination.

Therefore, it is free from the characteristics of mind and objects, and no phenomena can appear therein. If there were cognitive illumination, then phenomena could appear, just as when a mirror reflects objects, conditions for appearance arise.
The second is the mirror of causal perfuming. It is called "as-it-is and not empty," for all worldly objects appear within it.
They neither emerge nor enter; they are neither lost nor destroyed. They abide eternally within the one mind, because all phenomena are identical with true reality.
Furthermore, it cannot be defiled by any defiled dharmas; the essence of wisdom is immovable and is fully endowed with untainted perfuming.
"Because of sentient beings.

This indicates and explains the mirror of causal perfuming (*hetu-vāsanā*). Regarding the "mirror of causal perfuming," it means that the non-empty essence and characteristics serve as the internal cause for perfuming.
This has two meanings. The phrase "perfuming according to reality" below refers to the first meaning. Indeed...
Just as the substance of a mirror is not empty, yet all worldly objects appear within it, so too the mind manifests objects; yet these objects are entirely the mind itself.
In reality, there is neither subject nor object, and thus there is no coming forth or entering, nor any loss or destruction. It abides eternally as the one mind.
The phrase "because all [is below]" explains that phenomena are identical to the mind. This is like a mirror whose substance is not empty, yet within which the myriad forms appear. Mirror...
Although images appear, the entire image is the mirror; thus, there is likewise no coming or going, nor any loss or destruction.

By relying on this non-empty essence and characteristic, one constantly perfumes [the mind), thereby enabling sentient beings to realize that phenomena are themselves the truth and to accord with the principle of suchness.
Just as by constantly perfuming a mirror-image, one causes people to realize that the image is fundamentally empty and to awaken to the mirror of reality as it is.
Furthermore, "all [lower realms]" and so forth refers to the second meaning: that the essence of wisdom is immovable and is not defiled by defiled phenomena.
And yet, it is able to be fully endowed with the marks of untainted virtue (*anāsrava-guṇa*).
Just as the substance of a mirror remains unmoving and is not defiled by impurities, yet is able to be fully endowed with all its various images;

so too, by relying on this unmoving essential nature and through constant perfuming (*vāsanā*), it causes sentient beings to awaken to impermanence, to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death, and to joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*. It is like using the images in a mirror [to teach] constantly...
Constantly perfuming [the mind], it causes people to perceive the transformation of their physical appearance, thereby leading them to abandon the provisional and seek the real.

Thus, in the former case, taking "suchness" (*tathatā*) as its essence and "objects" as its characteristic, the characteristic is identical to the essence; therefore, it constitutes internal perfuming.

In this [latter] case, taking "fundamental wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*) as its essence and "merits" as its characteristic, the characteristic does not differ from the essence; this also constitutes internal perfuming. This is what is described below.
This refers to the perfuming of the self-substance and its characteristics.

Third is the mirror of the emergence of dharmas. This refers to the non-empty dharmas, which emerge from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge, and are free from the signs of conjunction.

Because it is pure and luminous, this indicates and explains the mirror of the transcendence of dharmas (*dharmaviniḥsṛta-maṇḍala*). As for the "mirror of the transcendence of dharmas," it refers to the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).

Through the power of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*), it emerges from obstructions and leaves behind defilements; its wisdom is luminous and purely refined, like a bright mirror that has been polished.
Free from defilement, its radiance is brilliantly clear; thus it is called the "Mirror of the Dharma’s Transcendence. This is identical to the previously mentioned "Aspect of Wisdom-Purity.

Fourth is the "Mirror of Conditioned Habituation": because it relies on the transcendence of the Dharma, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness by manifesting according to their thoughts.
This indicates and explains the "mirror of the perfuming conditions.

Regarding the "mirror of the perfuming conditions," it means that based on the previously mentioned True Suchness (tathatā), having emerged from obstructions and become free from defilement, the light of wisdom is perfectly luminous; thus, it is able to universally illumine the minds of sentient beings.

Just as a mirror, when free from defilement, is able to clearly reflect all things, so too, although it universally illumines with its radiance, it is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and although it is capable of...

While the mirror-like essence is fundamentally quiescent and without activity, it does not obstruct the manifestation of various perceptions and auditions according to the capacities of beings, which differ from one another.

Just as a mirror reflects images differently according to whether they are beautiful or ugly, so too is it said that the cultivation of roots of goodness leads to manifestations appearing in accordance with one's thoughts.
This is the great function of True Suchness (Tathatā), acting as an external condition for the熏习 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is called the "mirror of the perfuming of conditions," which is precisely the aforementioned phase of inconceivable activity. The explanation of the meaning of returning to cessation is now complete.
As for what is called the meaning of non-awakening: it refers to not knowing, as they truly are, that the *tathatā* (suchness) and phenomena are one; thus, the mind arises through non-awakening.

Yet there is this thought. Thought has no intrinsic characteristic of its own; it does not depart from original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). It is like a person who becomes lost by relying on the directions: if one were to leave the directions, there would be no loss.
Sentient beings are likewise: they become deluded by relying on awakening. If one were to leave the nature of awakening, [there would be no delusion].

Thus, there is nothing that is not non-enlightenment. Because of the existence of the deluded mind of non-enlightenment, one is able to know names and meanings, and for its sake, true enlightenment is explained.
If one were separated from the mind of non-enlightenment, there would be no self-characteristic of true enlightenment that could be explained.
This clarifies that non-enlightenment arises based on enlightenment, and that enlightenment is spoken of in dependence upon non-enlightenment.

The first phrase cites the heading; the section beginning with "not knowing according to reality" explains its characteristics. Essentially, the true suchness of original enlightenment is equal and non-dual.

To know it is called enlightenment; enlightenment is precisely the absence of thought. Because one does not know according to reality, it is termed non-enlightenment. Due to this non-enlightenment, there is movement.
Thought arises from delusion; this is non-enlightenment arising in dependence upon enlightenment, and thought arising in dependence upon non-thought.

Yet this movement of thought through non-enlightenment arises by depending on fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi); therefore, thought has no self-characteristic and does not depart from fundamental enlightenment.

To clarify this, the following provides an analogy; the subsequent section on "the masses of beings" uses the Dharma to correspond with and manifest the meaning, thereby illustrating the nature of enlightenment.
"Delusion" (*mí*) is a metaphor for "non-awakening" (*bùjué*). The remainder of the text is self-evident. The passage beginning with "Because there is...

clarifies that true awakening (*zhēnjué*) is spoken of in dependence upon non-awakening. However, the general purport of the treatise is to clarify that awakening and non-awakening exist in mutual dependence;

they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are both ultimately ungraspable. Thus, the Tang translation states: "Yet that non-awakening has no reality of its own and does not depart from original awakening (*benjue*)."
Furthermore, one waits for the absence of non-awakening in order to speak of true awakening. Once non-awakening is gone, true awakening is also discarded.
This is what is meant by "using the false to reveal the various truths; both the false and the true are equally false."
Furthermore, based on non-awakening (*abodha*), three kinds of characteristics arise, which are associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening.

What are these three? First is the characteristic of the activity of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*). Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves; this movement is called "activity. If there were awakening, there would be no movement.
Movement entails suffering, for the fruit is never separate from its cause. Second is the characteristic of the capacity for seeing (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*). This arises because it relies on movement.
Therefore, seeing exists; without movement, there is no seeing. Third is the characteristic of the objective realm: because it depends on the capacity for seeing, the objective realm appears falsely.
Apart from seeing, there is no objective realm.
The preceding section clarified how non-awakening arises based on awakening; this section clarifies how the three characteristics arise based on non-awakening.

Regarding the "characteristic of the activity of ignorance" (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the mind's deluded movement based upon the non-awakening of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is designated as "activity.

This is because movement and action are termed "activity. Regarding the phrase "if one awakens, there is no movement": this is stated by way of contrast to establish the point. That is to say, if one awakens...
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is itself the absence of stirring thoughts. To know that one is currently stirring [the mind] is due solely to non-awakening (*abodha*).

When it is said that "stirring results in the fruit of suffering which does not depart from its cause," this refers to that which acts as the cause, namely karma (*karman*). This means that the sufferings of the two kinds of birth-and-death are all produced by the stirring of thoughts;
thus, the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) serves as the cause for the fruit of suffering. Therefore, it is said that the fruit [does not depart from the cause].

First, they are separated from their cause. Second, that which is "below" refers to the capacity to see, which exists because it arises dependent upon the movement of thought; therefore, if there is no movement, it does not exist.

The objective realm likewise exists dependent upon the capacity to see; therefore, apart from seeing, it also does not exist. Thus, one knows that these three, although spoken of in a sequence, arise simultaneously as mutual dependencies;
consequently, they are inseparable from non-awakening. Because they are inseparable, they do not [exist independently].
When ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, these three likewise cease. Therefore, it was stated previously: "If ignorance ceases, the continuity (*saṃtati*) ceases.
By "continuity," one refers to these three characteristics—karma and so forth—which arise in mutual dependence and proceed without interruption;
hence they are called "continuous."
Because there are objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), six further characteristics arise. What are these six? First is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Based upon objective conditions, the mind gives rise to discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant. Second is the characteristic of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*). Based upon cognition, it produces suffering and pleasure;
the perceiving mind gives rise to thoughts that correspond [to them] without interruption. Third is the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*). Based upon...
1) The characteristic of continuity: because the mind gives rise to attachment by dwelling upon and recollecting objects within the continuum of experience, thereby sustaining suffering and pleasure.

2) The characteristic of false discrimination: based on deluded grasping, one discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and speech. 3) The characteristic of the appearance of names: based on deluded grasping, one discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and speech. 4) The characteristic of the appearance of names: based on deluded grasping, one discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and speech. 5) The characteristic of the arising of karma:

based on names, one seeks after them and grasps at them, thereby creating various kinds of karma. 6) The characteristic of suffering bound by karma: because one undergoes [retribution] based on karma.
It is replied: Because there is no self-mastery, one should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled dharmas, for all defiled dharmas are characterized by non-awakening.

This section investigates and explains the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), concluding by returning to the fundamental principle. The first two lines recapitulate the preceding general heading.

The section beginning with "How so? investigates and explains the six characteristics. The section beginning with "It should be known" concludes by returning to the fundamental principle. As for the term "characteristic of wisdom" (*jñānalakṣaṇa*):

This refers to not realizing that the previously manifested objects are false and illusory; within the state of signlessness, one falsely gives rise to the conceptualization of signs of favorability and unfavorability.
Therefore, it is called the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). As for the "characteristic of continuity" (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*):

it refers to the mind giving rise to joy and pleasure toward the previously conceptualized objects of favorable attachment, and giving rise to sorrow and suffering toward unfavorable objects of non-attachment; thus, one dwells upon these signs of favorability and unfavorability, and of suffering and pleasure.
The characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the uninterrupted connection with mindfulness.

The characteristic of grasping (*udgraha-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the mind that dwells upon and maintains feelings of suffering and pleasure regarding the objects previously perceived through mindfulness—whether favorable or unfavorable—and which, failing to realize their emptiness, gives rise to deep attachment;
this is called the characteristic of grasping. The characteristic of calculating names (*nāman-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to relying on the deluded mind previously grasped.
Regarding the "object": it refers to the conceptualization of the signs of provisional names and words; this is called the "sign of calculating names.

As for the four signs mentioned above, if they are correlated with the two types of grasping—grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena—the first two belong to grasping at phenomena, and the latter two belong to grasping at a self.

If they are correlated with the three categories of afflictions, karma, and suffering, all four signs belong to afflictions; the latter two are precisely the signs of karma and suffering. Regarding the "sign of initiating karma," this refers to [the state] prior to...
The conceptualized signs of provisional names and words lead one to seek out names and grasp at them, thereby activating body and speech to create various kinds of karma;

this is called the "characteristic of initiating karma. As for the "characteristic of being bound by karma and suffering," it refers to experiencing the retributions of pleasure and pain based on previously created karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—and thus transmigrating through the three realms, long fettered in birth and death without autonomy; hence, it is called "being bound by karma."

The characteristic of suffering. The nine characteristics mentioned above, though differing in their coarseness or subtlety and distinct in their respective objects and mental states, all arise because fundamental ignorance fails to comprehend True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is said that ignorance can give rise to all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). The phrase "Because all...
and following explains the reason why ignorance gives rise to phenomena; this is because the three subtle and six coarse [characteristics] collectively encompass them all.
Regarding all defiled dharmas: although defiled dharmas are numerous, they are all manifestations of the differentiation of non-awakening.
Thus, one knows that all defiled dharmas arise from ignorance. The explanation of the meaning of the arising of illumination is complete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of characteristics regarding awakening and non-awakening. What are these two? First, the characteristic of similarity; second, the characteristic of difference.

As for the characteristic of similarity: just as various earthenware vessels all share the same nature and characteristics of fine dust, so too do the various illusory manifestations of karma—whether outflow-free or characterized by ignorance—all share the same nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, in the *Sūtra*, based on...
Regarding this meaning, it is said that all sentient beings are from the beginning eternally abiding in *nirvāṇa*.

The Dharma of *bodhi* is neither a characteristic to be cultivated nor a characteristic to be produced; ultimately there is nothing to be attained, nor is there any form or characteristic to be perceived.
Yet, those who perceive forms and characteristics do so only because they follow the illusory workings of defiled karma; these are not the nature of non-empty wisdom-form.

Because the characteristic of wisdom cannot be perceived as something distinct. As for the characteristic of difference: just as various earthenware vessels are each different from one another, so too are the outflows-free and the ignorant differentiated by the delusive manifestations of defilement;
they are differentiated by the delusive manifestations of their own nature’s defilement.

This citation of analogies clarifies the characteristics of the identity and difference between awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*). Furthermore, the section beginning with "Next" provides a general heading for the two characteristics.

The section beginning with "How so" interrogates and enumerates the two characteristics. The section beginning with "The characteristic of identity" cites analogies to explain and establish these two characteristics.

Regarding the "characteristic of identity," it is said: for example, like earthenware vessels; although they differ individually in terms of refinement or coarseness, their fundamental nature and appearance—

This is distinct from the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*). It serves as an analogy for the fact that fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*), which is untainted (*anāsrava*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), which is tainted (*sāsrava*), differ in their various characteristics and functions—whether defiled or pure—and yet their essential nature and appearance are both identical to *tathatā* (suchness).

Therefore, it is called "the same aspect" (*samāna-lakṣaṇa*). Because these defiled and pure characteristics and functions are all identical to *tathatā*, the sūtras rely on this meaning of sameness to speak of the [multitude].
Birth is fundamentally nirvana; bodhi is not something to be attained through cultivation, nor is there any characteristic to be perceived. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvana; they do not undergo further extinction. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says:

The supremely pure and luminous mind is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others. Why, then, rely upon arduous effort or the cultivation and realization of subtle refinements?

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "That nature of perfect enlightenment is not something attained through action. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There is no wisdom and no attainment. Furthermore, another sūtra states:
"The fruit of Buddhahood possesses no forms, sounds, or meritorious qualities; it is solely suchness and the suchness of suchness."

Wisdom alone remains. Since it possesses no forms or sounds as its attributes, yet there are those who perceive visible forms, this is solely due to the illusory power produced by the defiled karma of sentient beings;
it is not that the nature of wisdom itself possesses visible forms. This is because the characteristics of wisdom are such that nothing can be seen.
Regarding the section on "differentiation," first the metaphor is used to clarify the difference, followed by the application of the teaching to illustrate it. As for the phrase "earthenware vessel":
The phrase "various and different" serves as an analogy for the distinct characteristics and functions of defilement and purity, each being individually differentiated.

Regarding the statement "differences according to the illusory transformations of defilement," it means that the characteristics of immeasurable pure merits are all established by reversing [the states of] defilement. Thus, it was said previously:
"The characteristic of the mind’s continuity ceases, and the characteristic of the purity of wisdom arises. It will be stated below: "If the mind has movement, it possesses faults."
Regarding the meaning of the delusory defilements, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges:

because the nature of the mind is unmoving in relation to these meanings, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of various pure merits, also as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This explains the differentiation of illusory manifestations according to defilement by way of their meritorious characteristics.
As for their functional application, although the aspect of wisdom is invisible, it nevertheless manifests in accordance with the defiled karma of sentient beings.
What is seen through the power of illusion possesses inherently different colors and forms as karmic retributions;
therefore, it was said previously that they appear in various ways according to the faculties of sentient beings, naturally corresponding to them so that they may obtain benefit.

Regarding the statement "the nature is defiled by the distinctions of illusion," this refers to all delusional defilements—the three subtleties and six gross states—which all arise because ignorance deludes the principle of equality.
Therefore, their natures are inherently differentiated. Thus, the subsequent passage states: "True Suchness is fundamentally one, yet there are immeasurable and boundless instances of ignorance;
from the very beginning, their self-nature has been differentiated. Hence, it is said that the nature is defiled and illusory, and thus differentiated.

Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing: it refers to the fact that sentient beings evolve in dependence upon mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). What is the meaning of this?
Because one relies upon the *ālayavijñāna*, ignorance is said to exist; through non-awakening, it arises, enabling both seeing and manifestation.
Because it is able to grasp objects and gives rise to a continuous stream of thought, it is called "mind" (*manas*).

This clarifies the meaning of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing, thereby explaining the "causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind" from the section on the Establishment of the Meaning.
The first phrase summarizes the preceding chapter; the words "namely" (*yǐwèi*) and below specifically clarify the causes and conditions for arising. It says:
Regarding the causes and conditions for arising: fundamental awakening (*mūla-avabodha*) acts as the cause, and non-awakening (*an-avabodha*) acts as the condition.

Through the conjunction of these two, the mind (*manas*) and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) arise. Since this arising is explained in relation to sentient beings, it is said that "sentient beings revolve based on the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness.
"Revolving" (*vartate*) means "arising. Below this point, the text raises a question regarding the aforementioned meaning, namely: "What is this that depends on the mind?"
Regarding the meaning of "the transformation of mind, intellect, and consciousness," the following section explains and establishes the preceding point. Question:

Previously it was stated that "based on awakening (bodhi), there is non-awakening (abodhi)"; why is it now said that "based on the ālayavijñāna, there is ignorance (avidyā)"? Answer: The essence of the ālayavijñāna is itself the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, when it is said here that "based on the ālayavijñāna, there is ignorance," it means that [ignorance] exists based on the Tathāgatagarbha.
Because of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no contradiction. To say that it "arises from non-awakening" means that the mind falsely arises based on non-awakening.

This arising is movement; movement is the mark of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). The ability to see and the ability to manifest are the two marks of transformation and manifestation (*pariṇāma-vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*).

The ability to grasp objects and the arising of continuous thoughts are the mark of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the mark of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called the "mind" (*manas*).
To summarize the preceding meaning: the reason why "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) is not explicitly mentioned will be fully explained in the subsequent text.

Thus, based on awakening (*bodhi*), there is non-awakening (*abodhi*); based on non-awakening, the three subtle and four coarse [evolutions] are initiated. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings revolve according to mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Now, while this [passage] speaks of the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*) based on the *ālayavijñāna*, the previous section spoke only of being "based on mind. This is because the text...
This is merely an abbreviated expression. For a solitary reality does not give rise [to consciousness]; it is only when reality and delusion combine that the mental faculty can arise.
Therefore, while the preceding passage spoke of "relying on the mind," this one speaks of "relying on the ālayavijñāna because of the presence of ignorance."
This mind further has five names. What are the five? First, it is called the *karma-vijñāna* (action-consciousness), because by the power of ignorance, the mind moves without awareness.
Second, it is called the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving-consciousness), because based on the moving mind, one is able to perceive appearances.
The third is called the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*). This refers to that which can manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images;
the manifesting consciousness is likewise. In accordance with the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), it manifests immediately upon their encounter, without any sequence of before or after.

Because it arises spontaneously at all times, it is always present in front [of the other consciousnesses]. The fourth is called the cognitive consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), which refers to the discrimination of defilement...
Because it is a pure dharma. Fifth, it is called the *saṃtati-vijñāna* (continuum-consciousness).
Because it is associated with mindfulness and is uninterrupted, it maintains and upholds the wholesome and unwholesome karma of immeasurable past lives so that it is not lost.
Furthermore, it can bring to maturity the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error. It can cause events already experienced in the present to suddenly...
Contemplate that future matters are not perceived through deluded thoughts; therefore, the three realms are illusory, being produced solely by the mind.
Apart from the mind, the objects of the six sense-fields do not exist.
This provides a detailed explanation of the five meanings, concluding by returning them to the single mind. The first sentence provides a general heading for the five names.

From "How so? below, the five characteristics are investigated and explained. Regarding what is called "karmic consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*): it refers to that which, due to beginningless ignorance, fails to realize *tathatā*.

When the mind moves falsely, it is called the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). Relying on this moving mind, it transforms into the faculty of seeing, which is called the *evolving consciousness* (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Relying on this faculty of seeing, all objects manifest, just as forms appear based upon a bright mirror; this is called the *manifesting consciousness* (*darśana-vijñāna*).
For just as a mirror does not manifest by itself but manifests in response to an object, so too the mind does not manifest by itself but manifests in response to an object.

It manifests immediately; therefore, it is said that "in accordance with the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), as they encounter [the senses], they manifest immediately, without any sequence of before or after.
However, since objects manifest due to the mind, this actually applies to all things. The mention of the "five objects" is merely citing the coarse and manifest to correspond to material forms.
From "Because all... onwards, the text explains the reason why they manifest immediately upon encountering them. For this manifesting consciousness, regarding a single...
It arises spontaneously at all times, unlike the sixth and seventh consciousnesses which are intermittent; thus it is said to be "always present before.
Because it is always present before, it manifests immediately upon encountering an object. These three characteristics above all belong to the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Therefore, it is called "subtle. From this point downward, it belongs to the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness); therefore, it is called "coarse.

As for what is termed *jñāna-vijñāna* (wisdom-consciousness), it refers to the spontaneous discrimination regarding phenomena that are either defiled or pure; this is named wisdom-consciousness. This is precisely the innate clinging to phenomena (*sahaja-dharmagrāha*).
As for the *anuvartaka-vijñāna* (continuing consciousness), it refers to the discriminating mind which, in every moment, [interacts] with defiled and pure phenomena...
It should be understood that what is called "continuous consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*) refers to its uninterrupted nature; this pertains to its own continuity.
Furthermore, it refers to the grasping at phenomena through discrimination (*vikalpa-dharma-grāha*). Regarding the phrase "maintaining [the seeds] below," this pertains to causing others to continue.

That is to say, the karmic actions—both wholesome and unwholesome—of immeasurable past lives are all moistened by the delusions arising from this consciousness, thereby causing them to be maintained and not lost. Thus, these are the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are capable of...
Moistened karma that has reached maturity does not perish; it is like water moistening a seed, preventing it from withering away.

Furthermore, regarding the retributions of suffering and pleasure—whether present or future—that have not yet matured, these are further moistened by the arising of delusions through this consciousness, causing them to reach maturity without fail.
Thus, afflictions are able to moisten unripened karma and cause it to ripen.
Therefore, it is able to bring to maturity the retributions of suffering, pleasure, and so forth, without error or discrepancy.

Furthermore, this consciousness is not only capable of ensuring that the karmic fruits of the three periods of time mature without loss, but it can also ensure that the thoughts and considerations regarding events already past or yet to come in the three periods do not perish.
For this reason, it is called the "continuing consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*). Thus, the following section concludes by returning [the discussion] to the single mind.
It is because of this movement of the mind that one is able to bring about the retributions of good and evil karma throughout the three periods of time.

Therefore, it is said that the triple world is illusory and is produced solely by the mind. As for the term "illusory," it means that the characteristics of the triple world are produced by the movement of the mind;
thus, they are empty and not real, false and not true. Since the triple world is created solely by the mind, if one were to depart from the movement of the mind—
Then there would be no objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). However, when following the process of the arising of bondage, one speaks only of the three realms (*tridhātu*);

yet when reversing that process toward cessation, one speaks only of the six sense-fields. These are merely different ways of expressing the same thing; in reality, both arising and ceasing apply universally to all things.
What is the meaning of this? It is because all dharmas arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thought.
All discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind; the mind does not see the mind, for no characteristic can be apprehended.
One should know that all worldly realms exist and are sustained solely by the ignorant, deluded mind of sentient beings. Therefore, all dharmas are like a mirror.

The middle image has no substance that can be apprehended; it is merely the false construction of the mind. This is because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
This interrogates and explains the meaning of arising and ceasing, clarifying that all phenomena arise and cease through the mind.
The first phrase interrogates the aforementioned meaning of arising and ceasing, asking: "How is it that objects are produced based on the mind, such that there are no objects apart from the mind?
The subsequent phrase, beginning with "Because," explains and establishes this point: namely, that phenomena cannot arise of themselves; they all proceed from mental conceptions.

Thus it arises. Therefore, it is said that the three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind. Since all phenomena arise from the mind, all conceptualization is simply the conceptualization of one’s own mind;
hence the sutra says, "The mind itself grasps the mind. Since one conceptualizes phenomena, one is conceptualizing the mind;
if one does not conceptualize the mind, then no characteristics can be apprehended. Thus it is said:

Apart from the mind, there are no objects of the six sense-fields. From this, one knows that all worldly objects are sustained by the power of ignorance and abide by relying upon the *karmic consciousness*.
Therefore, it is said that they all abide and are maintained based on the deluded mind of sentient beings' ignorance.
Since these phenomena abide and are maintained by depending on the deluded mind, then...
Dharmas have no intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said by way of analogy that they are like reflections in a mirror, whose substance cannot be apprehended.

Since their substance cannot be apprehended, one knows that all dharmas exist only as the delusive manifestations of the mind. Why is it that all dharmas exist only as the delusive manifestations of the mind?

"Because the mind arises below" explains why the delusive existence of the "mind-only" occurs, thereby concluding the cycle of arising and ceasing. This is because when the mind arises, phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Thus, one knows that all phenomena exist only as the delusive manifestations of the mind, and no substantial essence can be found.

Furthermore, as for what is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*): it is this very continuous consciousness which, based upon ordinary beings, becomes increasingly deep in its grasping and attachment;
it conceives of a self and what belongs to a self, engages in various false attachments, and, following after objects, discriminates the six sense-fields.

It is therefore named "mental consciousness," also termed "discriminating consciousness" (*prativikalpavijñāna*), and further called "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastuprativikalpavijñāna*). This consciousness increases in dependence upon the afflictions of views and craving.
This is because it establishes the long-term meaning.
This refers to the aforementioned consciousness, which clarifies the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

As for what is called "mental consciousness," it refers to the aforementioned consciousness that, based upon ordinary beings, engages in grasping, attachment, and conceptual fixation; it pursues objects according to circumstances and discriminates the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and is therefore named "mental consciousness."

This is simply the consciousness of the mind. Regarding the phrase "clinging and attachment deepen further," etc., it means that previously one failed to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and gave rise to false conceptualization;

now, however, not only does one fail to realize the emptiness of phenomena, but one further conceives of a self internally and what belongs to a self externally, or else engages in various false attachments such as [the self] being identical to or distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus, one knows that the former was merely the grasping of phenomena, whereas this...

Furthermore, because one clings to a self, it is said that "attachment becomes increasingly deep. Among the six coarse levels of consciousness, this refers specifically to the grasping at the characteristic of names.
As for what is called the "discriminating consciousness" (*vijñāna-vibhāga*), it means that previously, based on a single intention, one discriminates the six sense objects;

in terms of the subject that discriminates, it is named the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This [consciousness] relies upon the six faculties to separately grasp their respective objects; therefore, in terms of the objects being discriminated, it is so designated.
It is called the "consciousness that discriminates" (*prativijñapti-vijñāna*). Furthermore, it is also termed the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-prativikalpa-vijñāna*).

This means that while the former two primarily refer to the perception of present objects, this consciousness is able to universally perceive all kinds of phenomena across the three periods of time, as well as internal and external things;

therefore, it is called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena. Below this [level], based on afflictions (*kleśa*), it forms the "phenomenal consciousness" (*vastu-vijñāna*). This is because this consciousness relies upon views (*dṛṣṭi*)...
Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions of thought increase, it is called the "consciousness of phenomena" (*vastu-vijñāna*). Thus, the subsequent passage states:

"The habitual tendencies of the views and attachments that arise [therein] are so named because they can accomplish the meaning of the discriminative consciousness of phenomena. From this, one knows that the five modes of mentation (*pañca-manas*) all arise based on the habitual tendencies of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Therefore, the five modes of mentation and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are spoken of as being distinct from one another. However, this [distinction] depends upon...

The delusions and fetters are thus established. There are two intentions [behind this]: first, to demonstrate that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise through the perfuming of fundamental ignorance;
second, since the causes and conditions for arising have already been clarified, one now relies on the delusions and fetters in order to initiate the causes and conditions for cessation.
Regarding consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance: it cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can it be realized by the wisdom of the two vehicles.

It is said that based on a bodhisattva’s initial right faith, they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and investigate; yet even when they realize the Dharma-body, they attain only partial knowledge.
This remains so until the final stage of a bodhisattva, where they still cannot know it exhaustively; only a Buddha fully comprehends it.
This passage identifies that which is awakened and clarifies the differences between the modes of awakening; it briefly reveals the causes and conditions for returning to cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Regarding the "causes and conditions for returning to cessation," this means that intrinsic awakening (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*) acting as an internal perfuming is the cause, while the teacher’s instruction acting as an external perfuming is the condition.

Only when these causes and conditions are fully present can one give rise to understanding and engage in cultivation, thereby destroying delusions and entering the Path. The reason the text does not mention them here is because they were already discussed in the preceding two sections.

Since this has already been briefly clarified within the four mirrors, the following section—beginning with "based on ignorance"—raises the point that what is awakened to is beyond the scope of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles.

That is to say, consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*) can be known and perceived by ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles;

however, consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) are the five sense-consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). These are what the three stages of worthiness (*traya-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sanctity (*daśa-ārya-bhūmi*) observe and sever.

Therefore, one is unable to perceive [it]. "Based on the lower" refers to clearly understanding the stage of mental application (*manaskāra*) and the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-śukla-bodhisattva*). From the initial right faith, they know that the True is fundamentally existent and realize that the delusory is fundamentally empty; it is from this that they arouse the thought of enlightenment.

They cultivate the contemplation of Consciousness-only without external objects (*vijñaptimātra-nirālambana-darśana*) and observe Consciousness-only. Hence, it is said: "From the initial right faith."

This refers to the observation arising from the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*). The phrase "if one realizes" and below clarifies the partial knowledge attained on the stages (*bhūmi*). Only a Buddha knows it exhaustively;

that is to say, Bodhisattvas on the stages personally realize the *dharmakāya*, destroy ignorance and delusion, and sever the continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*), and thus they attain knowledge according to their respective degrees.
Even regarding the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness), even those at the ultimate stage cannot know it completely; therefore, only a Buddha [knows it fully].
It is exhausted. However, while this merely speaks of "thoroughly knowing" (*parijñāna*) and does not mention "distancing oneself," this is because knowing the illusion is itself the distancing.
Although the text does not explicitly state it, the meaning is necessarily complete.
Why is this? This mind has been pure by its very nature from the beginning; yet, because there is ignorance, it becomes defiled by that ignorance, resulting in a defiled mind.
Although there is a defiled mind, it remains eternally unchanging.

Therefore, this meaning can only be known by a Buddha, namely, that the nature of the mind is eternally free from thought, and for this reason it is called "unchanging. Because one does not realize even a single dharma...
Because it belongs to the realm (*dhātu*), it is dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*). That which suddenly arises as a thought is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
This interrogative inquiry seeks to clarify why it is difficult to know; it thus explains the two meanings of "unchanging ignorance" (*avikāra-avidyā*).

The first phrase interrogates the preceding meaning, asking: for what reason is this consciousness (*vijñāna*) knowable only by a Buddha? The section beginning with "This mind" provides the explanation.

The meaning that is difficult to understand refers to the fact that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Because one fails to awaken to this, there is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Once defiled by ignorance, there arises a defiled mind; this is what is meant by "being defiled while remaining undefiled," which is difficult to comprehend.
Although there is a defiled mind, this pure true mind is eternally constant and unchanging;
that is to say, it is "defiled yet undefiled," which is likewise difficult to comprehend. Therefore, the following section concludes by identifying the person capable of knowing this.
For the meaning of being "undefiled yet defiled" and "defiled yet undefiled" is profoundly deep and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to know; thus, [the stages] end here.
It cannot be fully known; only a Buddha can know it. This refers to the explanation of the two meanings of "immutable ignorance" (*amala-avidyā*).
Regarding "immutable": it means that the nature of the mind is pure and eternally free from thought; therefore, it is called immutable. Regarding "ignorance":
it means that if one realizes the *dharmadhātu*, then one is in accord with the true mind, and the mind does not move delusively.
It is not that ignorance does not exist; rather, because one does not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, it is dissociated from the mind.
The failure to awaken to the movement of thought is what is called ignorance.

There are six kinds of defiled minds (*saṃkliṣṭa-citta*). What are the six? First is the defilement associated with attachment (*abhiniveśa-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is abandoned through the liberation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and by departing from the stage of faith (*adhimukti-bhūmi*).

Second is the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anācchedya-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which can be gradually relinquished through the cultivation of skillful means on the stage of faith, until it is ultimately abandoned upon attaining the stage of pure mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*). Third is the defilement of partial... [text truncated]

1. The defilement associated with the distinct cognition (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) is gradually abandoned starting from the stage of possessing the precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*), up until its ultimate abandonment at the stage of the skillful means of signlessness (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*).
2. Fourth, the defilement dissociated from manifested form (*rūpa*) is abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā-bhūmi*). 3.
Fifth, the defilement dissociated from the seeing mind (*darśana-citta*) is abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over the mind (*citta-vaśitā-bhūmi*). 4. Sixth, the fundamental karma...
Non-associated defilements are abandoned by relying on the Bodhisattva’s stage of completion (*kṣayabhūmi*), because one is able to leave them behind upon entering the Tathāgata stage.
As for those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), they observe and train to sever them from the stage associated with faith (*śraddhāpratilambhabhūmi*);
they attain partial abandonment upon entering the stage of pure mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*), until finally attaining ultimate abandonment at the Tathāgata stage.

This provides a detailed demonstration of the characteristics of being free from the defilement of delusions according to the stages, and extensively clarifies the causes and conditions for returning to cessation (*pratyāgama*).

Regarding what is called "defilement associated with attachment" (*saṃprayoga-saṃkleśa*): it refers to the arbitrary arising of clinging and conceptualization based upon false objects; through the correspondence between mind and object, it defiles the pure nature (*viśuddha-svabhāva*).
This is called the defilement associated with attachment to names (*nāma-grāha-saṃprayukta-kleśa*). This refers precisely to the aforementioned mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because these six defilements consist of the preceding five [consciousnesses] and the mental consciousness, those at the lower stage of the Two Vehicles—referring to the liberation of the Two Vehicles and persons in the stages of the Three Worthies (*traya-ārya-pudgala*)—though differing in their Great or Small Vehicle status, are alike in having transcended the mental consciousness and alike in having severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
therefore, they are able to remain far removed from the defilement associated with attachment to names. Thus it is said.

"Correspondence with faith" refers to those from the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward; when the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) has matured and there is no longer any regression, it is called correspondence with faith.

"Correspondence with non-interruption" refers to the continuous and uninterrupted mental engagement (*citta-dharma-saṃprayoga*) that arises through false conceptualization due to a failure to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
this is what is meant by correspondence with non-interruption. This corresponds to the "continuity" among the five aspects of intention (*pañca-manas*).

This refers to "consciousness. Regarding the passage beginning with "based on association with faith" and below: it means that from the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward, one practices the expedient means of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and the absence of external objects (*anartha*).

By realizing that all phenomena are consciousness-only, one knows that there are no preceding [external] objects. Consequently, one is able to gradually abandon the conceptualization of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha-vikalpa*).

Upon reaching the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddha-bhūmi*), one becomes free from the signs of external objects and the conceptualization of the grasping at phenomena, which never again manifest; thus, one attains the ultimate.
It is far removed from and does not correspond with the defilements of continuity (*prabandha-kleśa*). Regarding the phrase "corresponding with discriminative cognition" (*vikalpa-jñāna*):
this refers to the state within the phenomena of defilement and purity where, although coarse discriminative grasping is absent, innate subtle afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) still persist;
thus, there remains a subtle discrimination regarding objects. This is termed "corresponding with discriminative cognition," which is precisely the *manovijñāna* among the five mental states.

Furthermore, regarding the section "Based on the possession of precepts" (*kṣānti*) and below: this refers to the stages from the seventh ground downward. Because the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is intermittent, there is a distinction between entering and emerging from contemplation;

thus, subtle discrimination still exists regarding objective spheres (*viṣaya*). However, as these [distinctions] are progressively eliminated stage by stage, it is said that one "gradually departs" [from them].
Indeed, from the eighth ground onward, there is no longer the distinction of emerging from contemplation to engage with objects; therefore, [this state] is exhausted at the seventh ground.

This is because it is deluded. Therefore, it is said that the stage of signless skillful means (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*) is ultimately free [from such delusion]. Regarding "possessing the precepts" (*śīlavant*):

because the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*) possesses the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), it is called "possessing the precepts. As for "signless skillful means": this refers to the signlessness of the eighth stage, which is devoid of the effort of skillful means;
whereas the signless contemplation of the seventh stage involves the skillful means of applied effort (*prayoga-upāya*) and possesses functional activity (*savyāpāra*).
For this reason, it is called the "expedient means of signlessness" (*animitta-upāya*). Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of form is non-corresponding":

this refers to the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*). Although this manifesting consciousness can manifest objects, as long as it has not yet given rise to discrimination (*vikalpa*), the mind and the object have not yet entered into correspondence;
thus, it is termed "non-corresponding. The passage beginning with "relying on form" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage who have already transcended the manifesting consciousness.
One attains the three kinds of mastery over the world according to the mind’s transformations, free from all obstacles; this is called mastery over name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vaśitā*).
Therefore, a sutra says: "One can manifest the body of a Buddha as the body of a sentient being, and likewise manifest the bodies of lands and so forth.

Since one relies on the stage of mastery over form, one is able to transcend the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); conversely, if one lacks mastery over form, it indicates that the manifesting consciousness has not yet been extinguished.
Regarding the statement that "the mind capable of seeing is non-associated," this refers to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Because these capacities for seeing have not yet manifested their objects, there is seeing without an object; this is termed "non-associated. Following the phrase "based on the mind":

it means that Bodhisattvas of the nine stages, having transcended the capacity for seeing, thoroughly understand the ten kinds of dense forests, such as the minds and afflictions of sentient beings; therefore, it is said they have attained mastery over the mind.

On this stage, one attains great mastery over the minds of others. Furthermore, because one has personally attained the forty kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), one skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma and extensively transforms sentient beings; this is called "mastery of mind. One attains great mastery over one's own mind.

Since one relies on this stage of mastery over the mind, one is able to transcend the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). By contrast, those who do not possess mastery over their own minds are revealed as being the opposite.

This means that the evolving consciousnesses have not yet ceased. Regarding the statement that the fundamental karma is non-associated: this refers to the karma-consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-vijñāna*).

It is called "fundamental karma" because the mind falsely moves due to a failure to comprehend *tathatā* (suchness). It is called "non-associated" because the aspects of seeing and perceived objects have not yet arisen.

The passage beginning with "based on the bodhisattvas" refers to the time when bodhisattvas at the lower stages, having exhausted their [delusions], leave behind the karma-consciousness and immediately enter Buddhahood.

Therefore, it is said that one attains entry into the Tathāgata-ground at the very end of the [Bodhisattva] grounds and is thus able to leave [the state of ignorance]; it is not that one leaves it only after becoming a Buddha.

As stated previously, "only a Buddha fully realizes [it]," yet when a Bodhisattva reaches the end of the grounds and knows the moment of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), they immediately enter the Buddha-ground.
Therefore, it is said that "only the Buddha thoroughly understands. This does not mean that one understands only after attaining Buddhahood.
The subsequent statement, "fundamental ignorance is ultimately abandoned at the stage of Tathāgata," also carries this same meaning.

Thus, we know that while the final mind of the tenth stage and the stage of Tathāgata are spoken of as two in terms of their conceptual definition (*artha*), they are non-dual in essence (*svabhāva*). The section below clarifies the abandonment [of ignorance] according to the stages.

Regarding the "characteristic of illumination" (*ābhāsa-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). One begins the process of observation, study, and severance prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Upon entering the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), one becomes separated from it; reaching the stage of the Tathāgata, one achieves ultimate separation.

Thus, although the six defilements of ignorance are described as occurring sequentially, their treatment and cessation occur simultaneously. This is because all six defilements take ignorance as their root; that is, they are none other than ignorance itself.

These are the characteristics of their differentiation. Therefore, when one is free from the six defilements, one is simultaneously free from ignorance; and when one is free from ignorance, one is simultaneously free from the six defilements.
Thus, there is no sequence of before and after. However, because the two meanings of "non-awakening" (*abodha*) and "activity" (*kriyā*) are distinct, they are divided into two.
Consequently, as explained in the subsequent text, the nature of the hindrance that obstructs wisdom is likewise distinct.

Regarding the meaning of "conformity" (*saṃprayoga*): it refers to the fact that while the mind, mental factors (*citta-dharma*), and objects are distinct, they are known to be identical in their characteristics of cognition and their characteristics as objects, based on the differentiation between defilement and purity.

Regarding the meaning of "non-conformity" (*asaṃprayoga*): it refers to the fact that the mind itself is non-awakened and remains eternally without distinction, and thus does not share the same characteristics of cognition and characteristics as objects.
This passage restates and explains the meaning of "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) and "non-associated" (*viprayukta*).

Regarding the meaning of "association," it refers to the fact that while the cognizing mind and the cognized phenomena are distinct from one another, they nevertheless function within the context of various dharmas differentiated by defilement and purity.

To be able to know that the two aspects of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) are identical means that they are identical despite being different; therefore, it is called "conjunction" (*samprayoga*).

As for what is meant by "identical," it refers to the mind perceiving defiled phenomena and immediately forming a defiled understanding, while the mind perceives pure phenomena and immediately forms a pure understanding;
because the mind and the phenomena are identical, it is termed "conjunction. Regarding the meaning of "non-conjunction," it refers to the True Mind not...

At the moment when the thought of awakening moves, although it can manifest objects, it has not yet engaged in the discrimination of those objects; thus, while there are objects, there is no [discriminating] mind.

Therefore, it is said that they are "always without distinction. This differs from the previous state where the characteristics of knowing and the characteristics of the objects were mutually conditioned; hence, it is called "non-associated."
Furthermore, the meaning of the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) is termed "hindrance of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā*.
The meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed "hindrance of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the spontaneously functioning wisdom of worldly activity. How is this so?
Because, based upon the defiled mind, one is able to perceive and manifest, falsely grasping at objects and thereby contravening the nature of equality. This is because all phenomena...

It is eternally quiescent and devoid of any characteristic of arising. Because ignorance is non-awakened and falsely opposes the Dharma, it is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects.

This demonstrates that the defiled mind, with ignorance as its obstruction, differs in its characteristics from the obstructions to wisdom. Furthermore, following the discussion of the defiled mind, it shows that the six types of defilement act as obstructions;

this refers to the meaning of how they obstruct the principle-wisdom (*prajñā*). That is to say, the six kinds of defiled minds are the obstructors, while True Suchness and fundamental wisdom are that which is obstructed.
This is because the clamor and agitation of the defiled mind obstruct fundamental wisdom; such is the nature of the defiled marks.
Distinction: It obstructs True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the six defilements agitate and disturb the tranquil nature;

therefore, the six defilements are called "obstructions of affliction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as they are able to obstruct the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of True Suchness. "Below 'Ignorance' (*avidyā')" indicates that ignorance constitutes the obstruction, in the sense of obstructing the wisdom of measure (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).
That is to say, fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) is the obstructor, while mundane karmic wisdom (*laukika-karma-jñāna*) [is what is obstructed].
This is precisely that which is obstructed. Because ignorance (*avidyā*) causes confusion and delusion, it is able to obstruct valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).
Due to this obstruction of cognition, one is unable to attain various cognitions that accord with worldly objects; therefore, ignorance is designated as "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is able to obstruct the "spontaneous wisdom of action" (*svayambhū-karmajñāna*) regarding the world. As for what is called "spontaneous wisdom of action," it refers to the world...

Objects of perception are known spontaneously, without depending on the application of thought; this is called the wisdom of natural activity (*svayambhū-karma-jñāna*). Regarding this point, the following section investigates and explains the preceding meaning:

"What is the meaning of these two obstacles that hinder wisdom? The subsequent passage, beginning with "Because it relies upon," explains the meaning of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) regarding the principle of wisdom (*jñāna-dharma*).
It states that the defiled mind is able to see and manifest—that is, the three types of non-associated defilements (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—which are falsely grasped.
The "objective realm" refers to the three types of defiled states associated with it; that is, these six defilements.

Through the distinction between subject and object, they contradict True Suchness (tathatā) by falsely grasping at objective realms and obstructing fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna). Thus, the defiled mind’s false grasping contradicts the nature of equality, thereby hindering the wisdom of principle and phenomena.
The phrase "Because all... explains the meaning of how ignorance obstructs the measure of wisdom. It says, "all dharmas."
Regarding the phrase "always quiescent and without arising," it means that all phenomena are eternally still, devoid of arising and ceasing. Thus, a sutra states:

"All phenomena are from the very beginning eternally and naturally quiescent. Due to ignorance, one fails to understand the quiescence of phenomena as they truly are, and thus falsely perceives arising and ceasing;
consequently, one deviates from the Dharma. Because one opposes the Dharma, one cannot accord with even a single aspect of the world.

Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that have the nature of perfuming (vāsanā), defiled and pure dharmas arise without interruption. What are they?
There are four: first, the pure dharma, called *tathatā* (suchness); second, all causes of defilement, called *avidyā* (ignorance);
third, the deluded mind, called the *karmic consciousness*; and fourth, the deluded objects, namely the six sense-fields.

yet because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of defilement arises. In the defiled dharma of ignorance, there is in reality no pure activity;
yet because it is perfumed by *tathatā*, the function of purity arises.

The preceding section clarified defilement and purity, as well as arising and ceasing; it was established that these processes of defiled and pure arising and ceasing necessarily occur through the mutual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the defiled and the pure.

As for intrinsic nature, it exists due to deluded vision, just as a person with cataracts sees hairs, moons, and so forth.

Knowing this, one then cultivates the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). By contemplating that all phenomena are consciousness-only, one distances oneself from the preceding objects. Thus the verse says: "Consciousness-only has no objective realm;
because there are no external objects, it is a deluded vision, like a person with cataracts seeing such things as hairs and moons. This...
Thus, by means of the previously mentioned aversion to [samsara] and the pursuit of purity, one nurtures and perfumes *tathatā* (suchness), thereby increasing its power.

Consequently, *tathatā* follows these pure conditions and once again gives rise to faith and understanding, cultivating the dharma of detachment. With the words "according to reality" (*yathābhūtam*) and below, the text reiterates the preceding point to clarify true cultivation;
