that is to say, because one cultivates the dharma of detachment prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one attains knowledge of non-existence according to reality.

"Regarding the preceding 'objective realm' (*viṣaya*): this refers back to what was stated above. As for the phrase 'various skillful means' (*upāya*) and so forth, this refers to the practices cultivated on the stages (*bhūmi*).

That is to say, because one realizes that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from stinginess and greed, one practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and the others in accordance with that realization.
Although one extensively cultivates the various perfections through manifold skillful means, there is no characteristic of grasping (*upalambha-lakṣaṇa*)."
Because one grasps through conceptualization, it is said that "one does not grasp and does not conceptualize. Cultivating in this manner for a vast number of kalpas, ignorance is extinguished.
Because ignorance is extinguished, the false mind and its objects, as well as the six defilements, are all extinguished accordingly.
Because all delusive defilements have been extinguished, it is called the attainment of nirvāṇa, wherein spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-karma*) is accomplished.
This arises from practicing in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), thereby transcending the characteristics of subject and object through the power of long-term cultivation.
Consequently, ignorance and the six types of defilement all vanish, and the essence and function of nirvāṇa manifest before one in vast clarity.
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are the two?

First is the perfuming of the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), which pertains to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who, weary of the suffering of birth and death, gradually advance toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities.
Second is the perfuming of the *manas* (intellect), which refers to all Bodhisattvas who, having generated a courageous resolve, swiftly advance toward Nirvana.
Because of this [delusion].

This section specifically clarifies the slowness or speed with which the perfuming of the deluded mind progresses toward awakening. Under the heading "the deluded mind," the number of categories is raised as an inquiry.

Under "the first," it clarifies the gradual process by which the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects) perfumes the True [Mind] and advances toward the Principle; that is to say, ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles do not...

Even if one realizes that all phenomena are mind-only, if the conceptualization of grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been extinguished, then one relies on the *vṛtti-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects) to permeate the True [Mind].
Although one uses the consciousness of objects to permeate the True [Mind], because one has not yet realized mind-only, one perceives the existence of birth and death as something to be loathed.

Nirvāṇa is worthy of aspiration; therefore, one moves toward great bodhi distantly and gradually. Second, the lower section clarifies the speed with which the five types of mental intention (*manas*) perfume the true nature of reality.
This refers to the three stages of worthiness (*traya-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa-ārya-bhūmi*).

Although they have realized that all is mind-only and are able to investigate according to the principle, because they have not yet abandoned the *manas*, they perfume the true nature with deluded mental intention. Even though they perfume the true nature with deluded mental intention, since—

Upon realizing that all is but mind, one forgets external conditions and illuminates within, thereby accords with the fundamental nature. Consequently, the arousal of the bodhicitta becomes courageous and fierce.
Because this arousal of the mind is so courageous and fierce, one approaches Great Nirvana with intimacy and speed.

Now, although the five types of intention (*pañca-manas*) are not mentioned, it is simply said that "the mind perfumes" (*manas-vāsanā*), because when those at the stage of the three levels of worthiness advance to the first ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*), they sever the *saṃtati-vijñāna* (the continuous consciousness). Thus...

There remain only four intentions up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), and finally only one intention remains. Because each stage is distinct, it is not said that there are five intentions, but rather that there is "the perfuming of the intention.
Question: Previously, it was stated that when the false perfumes the True, one transmigrates through birth and death;

why then is it said here that by depending on the perfuming of the false upon the True, one swiftly proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*? Answer: The former case was according to [the flow of] worldly conditions...

Because the defiled outflow perfumes [the mind], one transmigrates through birth and death. Because this relies on the perfuming of the pure function of the reverse flow, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
There are two meanings regarding the perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā*). What are these two? First, perfuming by its own essential nature; second, [perfuming by its attributes].

Regarding the perfuming by its own essence and characteristics: from time immemorial, it has been endowed with untainted dharmas and possesses inconceivable activity as the nature of the objective realm.
Based on these two meanings, it constantly perfumes [the mind].

Because it possesses this power, it can cause sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth and death and joyfully seek nirvana, and to have self-confidence that their own bodies possess the true [nature].
In accordance with the Dharma, one arouses the mind and practices.

This section specifically clarifies the permeation (*vāsanā*) of the essence and function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Herein, first, the permeation of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is explained.

Regarding "True Suchness," the number is stated and the items are enumerated. As for the phrase "permeation of its own essential nature": "essence" (*tattva*) refers to that which is capable of possessing the dharma-body; "nature" (*lakṣaṇa*)...
This refers to the characteristics of the untainted virtues it possesses, as well as the characteristics of its objective spheres.

However, in terms of their essential nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), they are like a jewel and its radiance, never being separated from one another; therefore, its essence is said to "possess untainted dharmas.

This is because its essence is endowed with the nature of untainted virtuous qualities. Thus, True Suchness (*tathatā*) constitutes the essence, while the virtuous qualities constitute the characteristics.
To say that "inconceivable activity is fully present" means that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is fully endowed with the internal function of permeation (*vāsanā*).

Regarding this activity as "inconceivable," it means that the true essence is without marks; ignorance has no inherent nature; and there is neither a resemblance nor a functional capacity for permeating.
Since it lacks an inherent nature, how could it have the capacity to receive permeation? Nevertheless, it does not preclude the true essence from being capable of permeating.
Delusion. Delusion receives the permeation of the True [Suchness]. This is the power of awakening permeating in a hidden manner, subtle and unfathomable;

therefore, it is called "inconceivable karma. This refers precisely to what is called "inconceivable permeation" below. As for the phrase "the nature that creates objective realms," this means that True Suchness acts as the nature that creates all objective realms.
Therefore, the characteristics do not differ from the nature. Because the characteristics do not differ from the nature...
Therefore, it can permeate ignorance; this takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its essence and its objective sphere as its characteristic.

Relying upon this essence and characteristic, it constantly permeates ignorance, thereby causing sentient beings to give rise to weariness with and longing for [samsara], and to produce faith and practice.

Question: If this is the meaning—that all sentient beings possess *tathatā* (suchness) equally and are all subject to perfuming (*vāsanā*)—why is there the distinction between having faith and lacking faith, and why are there immeasurable differences in temporal sequence?

Should not everyone simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess the *tathatā*-dharma, diligently cultivate skillful means, and equally enter *nirvāṇa*? Answer: Although *tathatā* is fundamentally one, it possesses immeasurable...

Regarding the ignorance of the extremes: from the very beginning, due to the differences in their intrinsic natures and their varying degrees of density, there arise distinctions among the supramundane afflictions numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, which all originate based on ignorance;
and there arise distinctions among the afflictions of self-view, attachment, and defilement, which also originate based on ignorance.
In this way, all such afflictions arise depending upon ignorance, with immeasurable distinctions occurring before and after.

Because only the Tathāgata can know this, he provides a question and answer to clarify that while true permeation (*tathatā-vāsanā*) is equal, there is inequality in faith-understanding, cultivation, and realization.
The section beginning with "Question" raises an objection regarding the equality of true permeation; it asks: if true permeation were equal for all, then for all sentient beings...

If all sentient beings possess *tathatā* (suchness) equally and it is uniformly permeated by habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*), then there should be no distinctions—such as existence or non-existence, greatness or smallness, or heterodoxy or orthodoxy—among their faith, understanding, practice, and realization.
Why, then, do there exist infinite differences such as having faith or lacking faith?
Furthermore, if these infinite differences were indeed uniform, everyone should simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess *tathatā* and diligently cultivate its realization.
[The stages] enter [into one another], and there should likewise be no distinction between preceding and succeeding. How, then, can there still be a distinction between preceding and succeeding?
However, the question posed in the treatise encompasses these two meanings;

it is merely that the translator’s phrasing was skillfully concise, first citing faith while omitting conduct and realization, and further placing an immeasurable number of phrases concerning preceding and succeeding distinctions in the middle, thereby comprehensively covering what precedes.

[The text] below causes the literary meaning to be unsmooth; therefore, the commentary supplements [the discussion of] faith, understanding, practice, and realization (*śraddhā-adhimukti-pratipatti-sākṣātkriyā*).
It then divides these into upper and lower sections based on two meanings: the immeasurable differences and the distinctions between earlier and later stages.

This is done so that there may be no fault of textual or semantic obstruction, nor the error of omitting any of the four dharmas. The answer begins with "Below," which refers to the inequality of afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
This is explained through the universal and the particular. That is to say, while True Suchness is fundamentally one, beginningless ignorance possesses immeasurable distinctions;
because its density and thinness differ, faith, understanding, practice, and so forth likewise possess immeasurable differences and sequential variations.
Thus, those with sharp faculties and thin afflictions have great faith and understanding, and their realization and entry are swift; those with dull faculties and thick afflictions are the opposite.
Therefore, they cannot be equal. The passage "more numerous than the sands of the Ganges" and below clarifies the characteristics of the distinctions among defiled afflictions.
Only the Buddha can know this. It means that although the sands of the Ganges are numerous, afflictions still exceed them;

hence it is said they "exceed those of the Ganges sands. These are the *rajas* (dust-like) delusions. The afflictions of self-view and attachment are the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*).
All such dust-like and view-and-thought afflictions arise based upon ignorance (*avidyā*). There is...
There are immeasurable distinctions between the preceding and the succeeding; although these are difficult to know even through noble wisdom, only a Buddha can know them.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; they are accomplished only when causes and conditions are fully assembled.
For example, the nature of fire within wood is the direct cause of fire, yet if no one knows it and no skillful means are employed, there is no possibility that it could spontaneously burn the wood.

It is impossible for sentient beings to do so. Although they possess the power of the perfuming of the true cause, if they do not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and others as external conditions, it is impossible for them to spontaneously sever their afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa*.
Likewise, even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming, [it is likewise impossible].
They are able to thoroughly weary of the suffering of birth and death and joyfully seek nirvana.

If the necessary conditions are fulfilled—namely, possessing the power of their own habitual cultivation and being protected by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—they are able to give rise to a mind that loathes suffering, believe in the existence of nirvana, and cultivate roots of goodness. Because these cultivated roots of goodness reach maturity, they then encounter...
It is only through the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas providing instruction, benefit, and joy that one can advance toward the path to Nirvana.
This addresses the previous objection by considering the mutual deficiency of causes and conditions. Furthermore, regarding the passage "The Buddhas... and so forth:

it means that for sentient beings to accomplish the Buddha-dharma, they must possess both cause and condition; if these are mutually deficient, it is difficult to accomplish. It is like [a piece of] wood...
Although the direct cause for fire exists, if it does not encounter the auxiliary conditions of the skillful means of drilling and kindling, it cannot burn wood.

Likewise, although sentient beings possess the direct cause and the permeation of practice, if they do not encounter the conditions of the Buddha and his teachings, they likewise cannot sever delusions and enter the Path.
Even if sentient beings possess the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharma lacks permeation, [liberation remains impossible].
Regarding "power" (*bala*): although one may have attained the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), one is still unable to ultimately advance in practice toward realization.
Consequently, there are immeasurable differences in faith, understanding, cultivation, and realization, as well as distinctions between earlier and later stages.

If one possesses the power of internal causal conditioning (*vāsanā*) and the condition of the Buddha’s sacred compassion and vows providing secret protection, one will naturally be able to give rise to the weariness with suffering.
With a mind that believes in the Dharma that liberates from suffering, one cultivates the roots of goodness.

Because these roots of goodness have reached maturity, one further encounters the Buddhas who provide instruction and guidance, thereby obtaining great benefit. With the arising of joy in the Dharma, one is thus able to advance toward the path of Nirvana.
That which functions as perfuming is the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions have immeasurable meanings;
briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are these two? First, the differentiated condition; second, the equalizing condition. Regarding the differentiated condition:
this person relies upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, from the initial moment they first resolve their minds and begin to seek the Way...
Until the attainment of Buddhahood, whether one sees or remembers [the Buddha] therein—whether as a member of the retinue, a parent, or a relative; or as a servant;

or as a friend; or as an enemy; or through the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—and even through all such immeasurable activities and conditions, by the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of great compassion, one is able to cause sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness. If...
Because one obtains benefit through seeing or hearing [the Dharma], these conditions are of two kinds. What are the two? First is the proximate condition, by which one attains liberation quickly;
second is the remote condition, by which one attains liberation after a long period. These two conditions, proximate and remote, are further distinguished into two types.
What are the two? First is the condition for increasing practice; second is the condition for receiving the Path.
This section provides a general indication of the two conditions based on their function. First, it clarifies the condition of differentiation (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*).

Following the phrase "by means of the function of perfuming" (*yong xunxi*), the text refers back to the meaning of the perfuming by function. With the words "In this way," it introduces the detailed explanation by citing the brief summary.

Under the heading "How so," it interrogates and enumerates the two characteristics. Under "Differentiation," it elucidates the meaning of differentiation: that sentient beings rely upon external conditions to resolve their minds and seek the Path, and so forth.
Upon attaining Buddhahood, during that interval, whether one beholds His body or recollects His virtues, there are immeasurable variations;

therefore, they are called "distinctive conditions" (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*). What is meant by "distinctive" is that the conditions for sentient beings to enter the Way, as observed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, are each different.
Accordingly, He manifests His body for the sake of those to be transformed, appearing either as a Honored One or...

Whether humble, or acting in accordance with or against [the needs of beings], or by employing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), they manifest every possible conditioned activity and immeasurable practice without exception; hence it is called "differentiation.

Yet within this differentiation, there is nothing that does not employ non-conceptual compassion and wisdom to permeate sentient beings, thereby causing them to increase their roots of goodness. Whether seen or heard, [they bring about this result].
They obtain benefit. Yet, toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they are fundamentally without intentional mind and are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).

Therefore, though dwelling in a position of honor, they do not exalt themselves; though situated in a lowly position, they do not demean themselves. They act in accordance with others out of compliance rather than attachment; they respond to adversity without harboring resentment.

Thus we know that the distinction lies in the capacity of the recipient (*adhikāra*), and not in the response of the Buddha. This section on "conditions" follows the preceding section which clarified the distinctions in the functional activity of the transformer.

This clarifies the distinction between the duration—whether long or short—of the transformation. Generally speaking, those sentient beings to be transformed whose roots of goodness are mature attain liberation swiftly;
this constitutes the transforming agent acting as a proximate condition for those beings. Those whose roots of goodness are not yet mature attain liberation after a long period;
this constitutes the transforming agent acting as a remote condition for those beings. Furthermore, within these categories of near and far, if [the roots of goodness] are not yet...
For those who are practitioners, it causes their cultivation to increase; for those who have not yet received the Way, it causes them to realize the fruits of the Way.
Thus, while conditions such as the duration [of practice] differ according to the capacities of sentient beings, there is no difference in the capacity of the transformer (the Buddha).
Regarding impartial conditions: all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally vow to deliver all sentient beings.

Through natural perfuming, they never abandon this aspiration. By virtue of the power of their wisdom of the identical essence, they manifest karmic activities according to the needs of those who see or hear them.
This means that sentient beings rely upon samādhi to attain the equal vision of all Buddhas;
this is the citation and explanation of the "equal condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

As for what is called the "equal condition," it refers to the fact that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas vow to deliver all sentient beings, and thus constantly permeate them with their compassion and wisdom of identical essence (*sābhāva-karuṇā-prajñā*), never abandoning them. Because they do not abandon them...
Therefore, in accordance with what each sentient being ought to see and hear within their own minds, he manifests his activities.
This refers to the following: the correct explanation of the meaning of "equal conditions.

Previously, because the minds of the beings to be converted were scattered and dissimilar, the person who converts them was also seen to manifest various distinct activities. Here, however, because those to be converted rely upon samādhi, then—
Seeing the emanated [Buddha] is likewise without distinction; thus, according to sentient beings, they see the Buddha equally within their own minds.
One thereby knows that distinction and equality both reside in the capacity of the recipient (*kṣetra*), and not in the response (*nirmāṇa*).
This熏習 (kṣaṇa-vāsanā), consisting of essence and function, is further divided into two types. What are these two? First is that which is not yet associated [with non-conceptual wisdom].

This refers to ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; they practice by means of the power of faith through the perfuming of the manas and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because they have not yet attained a non-conceptual mind that is associated with the essence [of the Tathāgatagarbha], they have not yet attained mastery.
First is the practice of karma, because it accords with the activity [of wisdom]. Second is that which has already attained such accord;

this refers to the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who have attained non-conceptual mind and accord with the wisdom-activity of all Buddhas. Relying solely on the power of the Dharma, they naturally practice, perfuming True Suchness and thereby extinguishing ignorance.
This is based on two powers to clarify the correspondence and non-correspondence between essence and function. The first three phrases raise the number to provide a general inquiry.

"First," and so forth, clarifies non-correspondence; this refers to ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness, who, by means of deluded consciousness, permeate the True [Suchness] and practice based on the power of faith;
therefore, their practice does not yet correspond with the essence and function of True Suchness.
This is indeed so. For when deluded consciousness (*vikalpa*) discriminates, one has not yet realized the Truth; thus, one has not yet attained correspondence with the essence of non-discrimination.

Furthermore, because deluded consciousness involves effort, one has not yet reached the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); consequently, one has not yet attained the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) for free and sovereign practice.
Therefore, one has not yet attained correspondence with the wisdom and function of *tathatā*. The second section below clarifies the characteristics of that which has already been attained.
It is appropriate. This refers to Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body who have attained correspondence with the essence and function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because they advance and practice spontaneously by relying solely on the power of the Dharma, they attain correspondence with the essence and function of True Suchness.

Since true wisdom has no distinction, it is called the "power of the Dharma"; since true practice is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called "spontaneous. By means of this wisdom and practice, one perfumes [the mind].
By practicing *tathatā*, one attains the extinction of the delusions of ignorance and becomes congruent with the essence and function of all Buddhas.
Thus, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh, one is congruent with the true essence; from the eighth stage onward, one is congruent with the function of wisdom.
Furthermore, for ordinary beings prior to the stages, consciousness is predominant and wisdom is inferior; for the Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya, wisdom is predominant and consciousness is inferior.

Thus, there is the distinction between being "in accord" and "not yet in accord. This does not mean that those prior to the stages possess only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), while those on the stages possess only wisdom.
Furthermore, the defiled dharmas have been perfuming [the mind] uninterruptedly since beginningless time; this continues until the attainment of Buddhahood, after which they are severed.
The perfuming of pure dharmas, however, has no interruption and extends to the end of the future. What is the meaning of this?

Because the True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) manifests, giving rise to the perfuming of its functioning; therefore, it never ceases.
"Severed.
This clarifies the meaning of defilement and purity, and what is severed or not. Furthermore, below this, it clarifies that defiled phenomena have no beginning but do have an end.

That is to say, the defiled phenomenon of ignorance has perfumed the True [Nature] from time immemorial, continuing in succession without interruption, from the stage of faith and understanding through to...
To "attain Buddhahood" means to effect eternal severance. To say that there is severance after attaining Buddhahood means that at the very moment ignorance is severed, one attains Buddhahood;
because it is a single, eternal severance, it is said that "there is severance afterward. This does not mean that severance only begins after one has attained Buddhahood.
Regarding the phrase "pure dharmas," this clarifies that pure dharmas have neither beginning nor end. For the essence and function of pure dharmas proceed from...
From beginningless time, it has been constantly perfumed and will continue until the end of the future without interruption.

Regarding this point below, the question is raised as to whether there is cessation or no cessation: that is, how can it be said that while these defiled dharmas are subject to cessation, pure dharmas are not?
This is explained by the following passage: because the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind...

It is extinguished. Therefore, from ignorance until the attainment of Buddhahood, it is then forever severed. Once the deluded mind has been extinguished, the essence is revealed and the function manifests;
throughout the limits of the future, it constantly permeates sentient beings, and thus there is no cessation.

Furthermore, regarding the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*): it neither increases nor decreases for any ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, bodhisattvas, or Buddhas.
It is not born in the past limit, nor does it perish in the future limit; it is ultimately eternal and constant, having been so from the very beginning.
Its self-nature is fully endowed with all merits. That is to say: because its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light;

because it universally illumines the Dharma-realm; because it is the meaning of true and authentic cognition; because it is the meaning of the self-nature pure mind; because it is the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
and because it is the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty. It is thus fully endowed with [merits] exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
Because the sands are not separate from, not severed from, and not different from the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, and because they fulfill them without any deficiency in meaning,
it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and is also called the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*.

This clarifies the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*), thereby explaining the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" which demonstrates the essential nature and characteristics of the Mahāyāna.
For the essence of True Suchness is equal for both the noble and the ordinary; it does not increase through the awakening of the noble, nor does it decrease through the delusion of the ordinary.
When traced back to the past, there is no beginning; therefore, it is not born at a prior limit (*pūrvānta*). When examined to the future, there is no end;

therefore, it does not perish at a subsequent limit (*aparānta*). Because it is devoid of increase or decrease, birth or cessation, it is said to be ultimately eternal and constant. This clarifies the essence of *tathatā*.

From the phrase "from the beginning" (*mūlataḥ*) onwards, the virtuous characteristics of *tathatā* are clarified; that is to say, the self-essence of *tathatā* is fundamentally free from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because it is free from false views and the defilements of inverted perceptions and delusions, it is said to possess the meaning of "great wisdom and luminosity.

Because it exhausts the three periods of time without change, remains untainted amidst all sufferings, dwells among both the holy and the ordinary without being constrained, and passes through the nine stages of decay without being stained, it is said to possess the meanings of "permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Furthermore, it is devoid of the feverish afflictions of delusion.
There is no transition through karma, nor is there any bondage through retribution; therefore, it is said that there is the meaning of being pure, cool, unchanging, and sovereign.

As for the aforementioned merits that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), their measure exceeds the sands of the Ganges and is difficult to enumerate in full; hence, it is said that "it is fully endowed with such as these.
Because these merit-characteristics of the sands of the Ganges are not different from the true essence, it is said that they are "not separate" [from it].
Because it has continued in succession from beginningless time, it is said to be "uninterrupted. Because its essence and its manifestations are non-dual, it is said to be "not different.
It is a single nature manifesting as manifold aspects, and these manifold aspects are entirely that single nature; it cannot be conceived by measuring it through the categories of one or many.

Therefore, it is called "inconceivable. Because this is what the Buddha has realized, it is called "Buddha-dharma" (*buddhadharma*). Furthermore, because all marks of virtue are the unsurpassed dharma, it is called "Buddha-dharma.
Thus, the preceding text states: "The unsurpassed dharma is not empty; it accords with the *dharmadhātu*," and so forth.
Below that, the name is established based on the meaning of the fulfillment of pure virtues, thereby manifesting that its essence and marks are not [separate].

It is "separation" (*viveka*). This means that since all merits are already fully perfected in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and lack nothing, the essence itself is able to contain immeasurable inherent virtues and also serves as the basis for those immeasurable inherent virtues;
therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and also the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*. However, herein the primary point is to clarify that these are inherently present by nature.

Regarding the measurement of merit: the following section, based on the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), describes the transformation from defilement to purity;
it thereby clarifies the distinctions among the characteristics of merit as they arise through cultivation.
Question: It was stated above that the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses such various kinds of virtues? Answer: Although these meanings of various virtues truly exist, they lack any mark of differentiation;
they are identical in a single flavor, being nothing other than the one True Suchness. How is this so? Because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) and free from division.
Distinct characteristics. Therefore, there are no two.
This sets forth the question and answer to clarify that while the characteristics of the virtues are distinct, they are in fact non-distinct.

"Question" and below refers to the principle that the essence of the True Suchness Gate transcends all characteristics, using this to challenge the distinction between the characteristics of the virtues. "Answer" and below clarifies the characteristics of the virtues.

"Differentiation is itself non-differentiation. This answers the objection. For True Suchness (*tathatā*) is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), yet it is not obstructed by possessing characteristics;
its qualities and characteristics, though they possess form, do not hinder its being without form. Because it is without form, it is equal and of one flavor, being solely True Suchness.
Regarding this point, the following section raises a question concerning the aforementioned meaning: "How is it that this differentiation is itself non-differentiation?"

The phrase "because there is no inferior" explains and establishes the preceding meaning. This is because when the characteristics of virtue are themselves without characteristics, one is free from the characteristics of subject-object discrimination;
therefore, they are non-dual, being solely True Suchness (tathatā). Thus, it was stated previously that this is a realm beyond thought, accessible only through realization and correspondence.
Furthermore, by what principle can these distinctions be explained? They are shown by way of the arising and ceasing characteristics of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). How are they shown?
It is because all phenomena are fundamentally mind-only; in reality there is no thought, yet there is a deluded mind that, through non-awakening, gives rise to thoughts.

Because one perceives various objective realms, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the nature of the mind does not give rise [to perceptions], this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.

If the mind gives rise to views, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing. When the nature of the mind is free from views, this is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor...
I am not pure. When afflicted by heat and suffering, and subject to decay and change, one lacks sovereignty; thus, there exist meanings of false defilements as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In contrast to these meanings, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of various pure merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If the mind arises and perceives further phenomena that are worth recollecting, then there is deficiency.
Such pure dharmas and immeasurable merits are themselves the single mind, with nothing further to be contemplated;
therefore, they are complete and are called the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is based on the distinctions among the characteristics of arising, ceasing, and defilement, in order to manifest the distinctions among the pure virtues of *tathatā*.
The first two phrases inquire into the cause from which these distinctions arise; the subsequent two phrases indicate the fundamental basis upon which these distinctions rely.
In essence, True Suchness (tathatā) is without marks. Because it is stirred by the movement of non-awakening thought, various defiled marks appear.

In contrast to these false defilements, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, then the marks of various pure merits arise. Thus, awakening exists because of delusion, and purity is established in relation to defilement.

Therefore, the distinct characteristics of its meritorious qualities are clarified, which are demonstrated according to the marks of arising and ceasing within the karma-consciousness. That is to say, based on—
The characteristics of the arising and ceasing of karmic consciousness are demonstrated. How are they demonstrated? This is explained by the following passage:

"All dharmas are but mind; in reality, there is no thought. However, in order to manifest pure virtue by relying upon the defiled characteristics of moving thoughts, one first clarifies the state of non-thought and non-characteristic.

Thus it is said that all dharmas are but mind, yet in truth there is no thought. Because one gives rise to thought through non-awakening and perceives various objective realms, ignorance is spoken of in contrast [to awakening].
For this reason, the nature of the mind does not arise. Being free from deluded views, there is no ignorance; thus, there is the meaning of the great light of wisdom.
Because a moving mind gives rise to views, there is that which is not seen. When the nature of the mind is free from views, there is nothing that is not seen;
thus, there is the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm. "If the mind has movement" and so forth refers to relying on karma.
A general indication of consciousness: that which is the movement of the mind cognizing phenomena is precisely deluded conceptualization; therefore, it is not the cognition of true consciousness.
Because movement entails defilement, it lacks intrinsic nature. Thus, it possesses all manner of deluded and defiled characteristics, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
Because the nature of the mind is unmoving in relation to these marks, there is the manifestation of the marks of all pure merits, which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number.
Therefore, all marks of pure merit are displayed in dependence upon the defiled marks of the arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
If the mind arises [from this state], it is insufficient for the presence of thought; this clarifies that being free from thought is fulfillment.

This is the definition of "binding. That is to say, if the moving mind has not yet ceased and one further perceives dharmas external to the mind as objects of thought, then the marks of defilement are not yet exhausted;
thus, regarding pure virtues, there is still a deficiency. This clarifies that the mental dharmas have not yet perished.
The purity of virtue is not yet sufficient. Such pure dharmas possess immeasurable merit; this is itself the single mind (*ekacitta*).
When one no longer perceives any dharma outside the mind that can be recollected or sought, then defiled appearances are completely exhausted. Therefore, it is fulfilled.
This clarifies that both subject and object have perished, and the purity of virtue is thus fulfilled. Because it is fulfilled, then with respect to its own essence, it is able to...
Because it contains and relies upon immeasurable merit, it is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (tathatā), it refers to how all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, while originally on the stage of the causal ground, gave rise to great compassion.

They cultivate the various pāramitās, gather and transform sentient beings, and establish great vows, desiring to deliver and liberate all beings within the realm of sentient beings as far as it extends,
without limitation by the number of kalpas and until the end of the future, because they regard all sentient beings as their own bodies.
Furthermore, one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings. For what reason?
It is because one knows, as they truly are, that all sentient beings and one’s own body are equal in *tathatā* (suchness), being without distinction.

By means of such great skillful wisdom, one eliminates ignorance and perceives the original *dharmakāya*. Thereupon, inconceivable activities and various functions arise spontaneously. That is to say:
It is equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and pervades all places; furthermore, no characteristic of activity can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body and the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa-kāya*).

This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which has no sphere of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), is free from deliberate effort, and yet is called "activity" only because sentient beings obtain benefit according to their own seeing and hearing.

This clarifies the greatness of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), thereby explaining the "Great Vehicle's Function" (*mahāyāna-prayojana*) presented in the section on the Establishment of the Meaning.
The first sentence cites the heading. Under the words "That is to say," it first clarifies the causes of the great function—namely, compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice.
Under the words "Because there is such as this," it clarifies that through wisdom one destroys delusion; thus, while realizing the essence and giving rise to function, there is no mark of function.
"Why is this? [The text] below interrogates and explains the reason why [the previous practice] was useless, thereby concluding the name of the "Great Function.

For indeed, when the Tathāgata first resolved his mind while on the bodhisattva path, he made the welfare of sentient beings his primary concern. Thus, he bestowed happiness and extracted them from suffering, applying himself with compassion;
he gathered and transformed them, practicing through great deeds; and he sustained this for a long duration through deliverance, fortifying it with great vows. Being able to act in such a manner...
This is transformation and deliverance. That one does not grow weary over a long period is because one regards all sentient beings as identical to oneself.
Nevertheless, one does not grasp at the mark of delivering sentient beings. For what reason does one not grasp at such marks?
It is because one knows that sentient beings and oneself are equal in true suchness (*tathatā*), being without distinction. This, then, is to be detached from marks.
This is the characteristic; that is, it is sustained by great wisdom. Possessing such great wisdom of skillful means, one eliminates ignorance and perceives the original Dharma-body.
Spontaneously, there arises inconceivable function, which is equal to True Suchness and pervades all places.
Although this function, like the essence itself, is all-pervasive, no marks of function can be apprehended. Why is this? It is because:
The Tathāgata is exclusively the body of the wisdom-aspect of the Dharma-body, which is free from worldly conventional activities;
yet, because sentient beings obtain benefit through seeing and hearing him, this is precisely "non-activity as activity," and is therefore described as the "Great Activity."

This function is of two kinds. What are these two? First, that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).
Because they do not know that it is manifested by the *pariṇāma-vijñāna* (transforming consciousness), they perceive it as coming from outside;
they grasp at its physical dimensions and cannot know it exhaustively. Second, that which is based on the *karma-vijñāna* (consciousness of karma) refers to all Bodhisattvas from the beginning...
From the initial aspiration up to what is perceived by the mind of the Bodhisattva at the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), this is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya*.
This body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*); and these marks possess immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

The supporting fruits upon which it rests likewise possess immeasurable varieties of adornment. According to what is manifested, it is boundless and inexhaustible, transcending all marks of limitation.
According to what is appropriate, it is always able to be maintained, neither destroyed nor lost.
Such merits are all accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices (*anāsrava-caryā*) such as the *pāramitās*, as well as through the permeation of the inconceivable (*acintya*).
Because they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, they are called "retribution" (*vipāka*).

The preceding section clarified the cause to manifest the fruit, thereby generally demonstrating the great function. This section, based on the fruit, clarifies the cause and specifically elucidates its two functions.
The first two phrases cite the number and pose a general inquiry. "First," and so forth, specifically elucidates the two aspects;
that is to say, the Tathāgata’s wondrous function without conditions is like a bright mirror suspended upon a high terrace, where what sentient beings perceive differs according to their reflections.

Regarding the beauty or ugliness of people: for this reason, ordinary and inferior beings do not understand that [all is] mind-only (*cittamātra*). As long as their discriminative thought has not ceased, they perceive the Buddha based on the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects).
Thus, they see the marks of the Tathāgata’s manifested transformation; this is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

Because they do not know that the Buddha appears from the transformation-consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*) of themselves, they see him as coming from without. Consequently, they see the form manifested by the Tathāgata...
There are limits. Because one perceives form as having limits, one cannot fully know form that is without limits.

When a Bodhisattva thoroughly realizes that there is only mind (*cittamātra*) and the emotions of conceptual discrimination cease, they perceive the Buddha based on the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*); this is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Having realized that there is only mind, they know that all marks are merely manifestations of the mind; thus, they perceive the essence of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the physical form of the body.
The primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are adorned with various jewels; each is vast and immeasurable, and each accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and is immeasurable.

These are the manifestations of the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-sampad* and *upabhoga-sampad*) according to the capacities of beings. They are boundless, inexhaustible, and without limit.

Not only do the functions and characteristics of the primary and secondary retributions pervade everywhere, but they also constantly sustain and maintain themselves according to what is appropriate for beings, remaining indestructible and unimpaired.
This is because there are differences in capacity—some great and some small; in consciousness—some coarse and some subtle; and in insight—some superior and some inferior.
Consequently, their application results in retributive responses. This is just as heaven and earth are impartial, yet the myriad things act according to their own self-interest.

Thus, the following section clarifies the causes of the retributive function and concludes by naming it: that is to say, the aforementioned marks of meritorious reward all arise from the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.

It is formed by causal practice as well as the inconceivable perfuming of original enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*). Because it possesses immeasurable marks of bliss, it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary beings is its coarse form; according to the six realms of existence, each perceives it differently. Its seeds—
Because they are of diverse kinds and do not possess the characteristics of experiencing pleasure, they are said to be "appropriate.

Furthermore, that which is seen by Bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*) is seen only partially, because they have deep faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma. They know that matters such as the adornment of those physical forms neither come nor go;
they are free from spatial limits and manifest solely in dependence upon the mind, never departing from *tathatā*. However, this Bodhi...
Sāgaramegha still engages in conceptual discrimination because he has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

If he attains the pure mind, that which he perceives becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior until the final stage of the Bodhisattva grounds, where his vision reaches its ultimate consummation. If one is free from the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), there is no appearance of seeing;
for within the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas, there are no reciprocal perceptions of color-forms or mutual appearances of self and other.

This further clarifies that the functions of retribution and response differ, and it also reveals that the *dharmakāya* is free from the marks of functional activity. Furthermore, the following section clarifies that the application of function differs.

Although the preceding explanation of the application of function was general, encompassing both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, it did not distinguish between them due to differences in their respective perceptions;
therefore, this is clarified again here to differentiate between the ordinary and the sage. Specifically, this refers to the marks perceived by those of the Two Vehicles.

This is the Supreme Response Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). Ordinary beings perceive it according to their own kind; this is the Inferior Response Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Although the Buddha’s bodies are identical, what is perceived by each is distinct.
Because it does not possess the marks of experiencing pleasure, it is called a "response" (*nirmāṇa*). Furthermore, the following section clarifies that the retributive functions differ.
This is because, although the preceding clarification of retributive function applies generally to those of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages, there are still differences in what they perceive.
There is no distinction [between them]. Therefore, this is explained again here to distinguish their relative superiority.

That is to say, although the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness (trīṇi kṣānti) have faith and understanding in *tathatā* (suchness), they know that the characteristics of the adornments of both the environment (*niśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are all manifestations of mind alone, without coming or going, and without limits.
Nevertheless, because they have not yet abandoned the conceptualization of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*) and have not yet entered the *dharmakāya*, regarding...

The retributive function of the Tathāgata can only be seen in small measure. If one is free from the conceptualization of attachment to dharmas and attains the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*), then what is seen becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior.

Up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), the retributive function seen is most extremely subtle and wondrous, beyond which nothing surpasses it; therefore, it is called the ultimate vision. This does not mean a state of non-seeing or signlessness.
This constitutes the ultimate state. If one departs from the lower [levels], it clarifies that the Dharmakāya is free from characteristics.

This means that previously, by relying on the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), one perceives the characteristics of function, with distinctions of superiority and inferiority and differences among the heavens. Here, by departing from the karmic consciousness, there are no longer any perceived characteristics; therefore, there is only the single Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, there are no further material characteristics that can be perceived.
A question is asked: "If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is free from material characteristics, how is it able to manifest material characteristics? The answer is given:
Since this very *dharmakāya* is the substance of form (*rūpa*), it is able to manifest as form. "Body" (*kāya*) refers to the fact that from the very beginning, matter and mind have been non-dual.
Because the nature of matter is itself wisdom, the substance of matter is formless and is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*).
Because the nature of wisdom is itself matter, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) which pervades all places.

The following question and answer are set forth to clarify that while being free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no obstruction to the manifestation of characteristics. "Question: and below: this restates the preceding point to pose a query. It asks:

since the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is already free from material characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), how can it manifest the material characteristics of the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)? "Answer: and below: [the response follows].
I answer by way of the essence itself. This is because the Dharma-body is the essence of the retributive and transformational physical forms.

According to the capacities of beings—whether great or small—one perceives the marks of the retributive and transformational bodies within the state of marklessness; therefore, it is said that "it can manifest form," yet it is actually the capacity [of the being] that manifests it.

Regarding what is called "the lower": this explains and establishes the meaning of the "upper" by means of the non-duality of form and mind. Because form is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), appearance is itself the signless (*animitta*);
thus it is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). Because wisdom is itself form, the signless is itself appearance; thus it is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), which pervades all places.
Thus, while the Wisdom Body is signless, it is not obstructed from manifesting signs according to the capacities of beings. The Form Body (*rūpakāya*) possesses signs.
It does not hinder the fact that the Dharma-body is signless; thus one knows that the Wisdom-body and the Form-body are two yet non-dual.
Because they are non-dual, they can manifest form and appearance according to the perceptions of sentient beings.

The forms that appear have no boundaries; according to the mind, they can manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions, displaying immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable reward bodies (*vipākakāya*), and immeasurable adornments, each distinct from the others, yet all without boundaries and without obstructing one another.
This cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of mind and consciousness, because it is the meaning of the sovereign function of *tathatā*.
This refers to the manifestation of the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-ālambana-vyūha*) according to the capacities of beings, which are universally fused and unimpeded;

this concludes the exposition on the great function of *tathatā*. The first two phrases generally clarify the manifestation of signs according to capacity; from "according to the mind" (*sui xin*) onwards, they specifically clarify the manifestation according to capacity.
Regarding the phrase "the manifested forms have no boundaries": this means that because they are manifested based on the aforementioned Dharmakāya, they possess no boundaries.

Regarding the phrase "capable of manifesting according to the mind" and so forth: this means that while the Dharmakāya is free from marks (lakṣaṇa), it manifests the marks of the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya in accordance with the minds of sentient beings;
hence it is said to be "capable of manifesting according to the mind. Thus, one should know that the response is fundamentally without [independent] mind.

This is a manifestation according to the capacities of beings. The "worlds of the ten directions" and so forth refer to the characteristics of the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants as they appear according to those capacities.
Although these are each distinct, because they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they are all without limits.
Because they are without limits, these characteristics of the environment and its inhabitants each pervade the entire *dharmadhātu* without...
They do not obstruct one another; thus, the one and the many mutually pervade, and the small and the large are harmoniously integrated.

This is the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which can certainly not be known through the conceptual discrimination of the sentient beings' mind-consciousness. Therefore, it was previously called the "unconceivable aspect of activity" (*acintya-karma-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, this demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing.

This means that when one investigates the five aggregates (skandhas)—both form and mind—and the objects of the six sense-fields, they are ultimately devoid of thought. Because the mind has no form or characteristics, even if one seeks it throughout the ten directions, it can never be found.
It is like a person who, due to delusion, mistakes the east for the west; yet the directions themselves have not actually shifted. Sentient beings are just the same.

Due to the delusion of ignorance, one takes the mind to be thought; yet the mind is in reality unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain compliance and enter the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).
This instructs one to contemplate the root of arising and ceasing in order to enter True Suchness (*tathatā*). Above, two gates have already been explained separately;

here, one is again instructed to contemplate arising and ceasing to enter True Suchness because, were these two gates not explained separately, there would be no means to open up the faith and understanding of sentient beings, and were one not to observe arising and ceasing, there would be no means to awaken to and enter True Suchness.

Explanation precedes realization; such is the natural order of things (*dharmatā*). The Master of the Treatise skillfully demonstrates this, excelling therein. Now, this single passage contains the headings, the explanation, and the conclusion:

"Furthermore" introduces the heading; "That which is called" provides the explanation; and "If one is able to... offers the conclusion. Within the explanatory text, there are the elements of the subject (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamāna*), and the application (*anusandhi*):
"That which is called" constitutes the explanation by way of the Dharma; "Just as a person" clarifies it through an analogy; and "The multitude of beings... [concludes the application].

This is a combined exposition. That which is called "seeking out the ultimate absence of thought regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth" means to investigate their origin within the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
For the five aggregates—the objects of form and mind—are themselves the phenomena of arising and ceasing, while thought is the very root of arising and ceasing.
Now, this instruction to investigate the root of arising and ceasing is the Sage’s method for uprooting [delusion].
This is merely the intent of "blocking the source. Why? It means that all dharmas arise from mindfulness (*smṛti*).
If mindfulness does not arise, all dharmas naturally vanish. Therefore, the preceding text states: "If one is free from mental thought, then there are no signs of any objective realms.
Is this not precisely the intent of uprooting the foundation and blocking the source? The passage beginning with "By means of the mind" explains the reason for non-mindfulness. Why?
Is it because, when one investigates the five aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, they are ultimately without thought?

Since the mind has no form or characteristic, even if one searches for it throughout the ten directions, it can never be found; therefore, when investigating all phenomena, they are ultimately without thought.

The passage beginning with "It is like a person... cites a simile to illustrate this point. Although both passages explicitly manifest the absence of thought, their underlying intent contains the act of investigation. It is, for instance, like being lost in one's direction.
This means that although one takes east for west, the direction itself does not change; thus, seeking the west in the east, the west cannot be found.
This is a metaphor for the deluded mind, which takes the mind to be its thoughts. Since the mind is in reality unmoving, one seeks thoughts within all phenomena, yet ultimately no thought exists.
"If one can... and so forth refers to those who have not yet investigated: they are in opposition to the truth and have not yet departed from [delusion].
One who possesses thought does not know non-thought; therefore, by means of investigation and observation, one immediately attains conformity with it. Thus, it was said previously:
"If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are then heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
When thought ceases and defilements vanish, within the pure mind one realizes the mark of non-thought; thus, knowing that the mind is without thought, one enters True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it was previously stated that if one is free from thought, this is called "attaining entry.
Thus, knowing that the mind is without thought can only be known by those who have abandoned thought; it is not something known by others.
Regarding the antidote to false attachments: all false attachments depend upon the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). If one is free from the self, there are no false attachments.
This view of a self is of two kinds. What are these two? First, the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
This passage provides a general overview of the two types of grasping based on the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). The first sentence restates the preceding heading.
The section beginning with "All" clarifies the root of false grasping; for false grasping arises from false views, and false views, in turn, arise from the self.

Therefore, it is said that all false attachments depend upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Since these attachments exist because they rely on the self, if one is separated from the self, there will be no false attachments.
The phrase "This is the self" below serves as a general heading for the two views. As for the "view of a person-self" (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*):
This refers to the conventional designation of a "person" based on the aggregation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The term "self" (*ātman*) carries the sense of a sovereign controller.
Failing to realize that there is no real controller within the five aggregates, one clings to the existence of a real self within them;

furthermore, based upon this, one falsely gives rise to distorted views, which are termed the "view of a self in persons" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This explanation is intended for beginners and ordinary worldlings who have not yet eliminated the notion of a personal self.

This is not discussed from the perspective of what they themselves maintain. Regarding the term "view of self in phenomena" (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*): "phenomena" refers to the dharmas such as the five aggregates.
Because one fails to realize that these lack a real, governing subject, one clings to all phenomena as being substantially existent;
furthermore, based upon this, one gives rise to a view regarding phenomena. Therefore, it is called the "view of self in phenomena."
Regarding the view of self and person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), it is said that there are five types based on the teachings for ordinary worldlings (*bāla*). What are these five?

First, having heard the *sūtra* state that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is ultimately quiescent and like empty space, because they do not understand that this is taught to destroy attachment, they claim that empty space itself is the nature of the Tathāgata.
How is this countered? By clarifying the characteristics of empty space. It is as follows: [text continues]
Delusory phenomena have no reality in their essence; they exist only in relation to form and possess the characteristic of being visible, causing the mind to undergo birth and extinction.
Since all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind, there is in truth no external form. If there were no form, then even the characteristic of empty space would not exist.
Thus, all objective realms exist solely because the deluded mind arises. If the mind is free from deluded movement, [these realms cease].
Then all objective realms cease, and there remains only the single true mind, which is omnipresent.
This is called the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast intrinsic wisdom; it is not like the characteristic of empty space.

This refutes the view that clings to emptiness as an inherent nature. The section beginning with "Person and Self" (人我) cites the enumeration [of categories] to raise the inquiry. The section beginning with "First" (一者) clarifies the conditions for the arising of such clinging;

it refers to those who, when the sūtras state that the *dharmakāya* is quiescent like empty space, fail to understand that the *dharmakāya* is tranquil and signless, and instead perceive the physical form and color of the Buddha as truly existent—it is for this reason that it is said thus. And...
Those who hear this do not understand that this parable is a teaching for the purpose of shattering attachments; they instead cling to empty space as being the nature of the Tathāgata.
The passage beginning with "How so? clarifies that the characteristics of emptiness are illusory. That is to say, the characteristic of empty space exists only through the delusion of form (*rūpa*);
it has no intrinsic substance from the beginning and is not real. Therefore, it is said to be a false phenomenon (*mṛṣādharma*), its essence being unsubstantial. This is the general [explanation].

This clarifies that the characteristics of space are illusory. Below, this is successively explained and established as illusory in order to refute false attachments and reveal the nature of the Tathāgata.
Why is space illusory? Is it not because its essence is unreal? This is answered by what follows. For space exists only in relation to form;
thus, it is illusory and lacks an intrinsic essence. It is a mental object of perception (*ālambana-nimitta*), and therefore is not real.
[Objection: "If it is real, why does it exist only in relation to form? Is its essence not unreal? [Response: This is explained by the following passage.
It is because form has no self-nature and is fundamentally mind. Since emptiness exists only in relation to form, and form is fundamentally non-existent, how could emptiness be obtainable?
Therefore, it is said: "If there were no form, then there would be no characteristic of empty space. Thus we know that [emptiness exists] in relation to...
As for the existence of form (*rūpa*), its essence is not non-substantial. Why is it that both form and emptiness are unobtainable?
This refers to the following explanation: all objective realms exist only because the mind is falsely stirred; if it does not stir, they do not exist.
Therefore, it cannot be apprehended. Since false objects do not exist, there is only the single true mind, which is omnipresent.
This is precisely the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast nature-wisdom; how could it be like the insentient characteristic of empty space?
Thus, the view that takes emptiness as an inherent nature is refuted.
Second, when one hears the sūtras state that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and true suchness are ultimately empty,
being primordially and inherently empty and devoid of all characteristics, to fail to understand this constitutes a refutation [of the truth].
Because of this attachment, one claims that the nature of *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa* is merely emptiness. How is this countered?
It is clarified that the self-substance of the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā* is not empty, for it is fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of intrinsic virtue (*guṇa*).
Third, when hearing the *sūtras* state that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases, and that its substance is complete with all dharmas of merit, because it...
Because it is explained as such, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Although there are distinctions among the characteristics of material and mental phenomena, how are these countered?

It is because they are taught solely by way of the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), while the distinctions are manifested through the teaching on the meaning of the defiled nature of arising and ceasing.
This refutes the view that [things] possess a nature of emptiness. Second, "Below" clarifies the conditions for the arising of attachment.
This refers to when the sūtras state that all phenomena, mundane and supramundane, up to and including *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa*, are primordially empty by nature and devoid of all characteristics;
yet, not knowing that what is taught consists of conventional designations and names rather than reality, one clings to these conventions as [ultimate truth].
This is precisely why it was stated thus. However, those who hear this do not understand that these words are intended to shatter attachments;
they instead cling to the view that the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) and *nirvāṇa* is merely emptiness. How is this to be remedied?

It is said that while the provisional names and marks of *tathatā*, *nirvāṇa*, and so forth are empty, the self-substance of *tathatā* and its intrinsically endowed virtuous qualities (*guṇa*) are not empty. How could this possibly be [otherwise]?

This refers to the emptiness of conventional characteristics. If one then asks whether the nature of ultimate reality is also empty, one falls into the erroneous view that clings to the nature itself as being empty.
Third, below, the conditions for the arising of such clinging are clarified.

This means that when hearing the sūtras state that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases and that its essence is fully endowed with all dharmas of merit, yet failing to understand the distinctions in the Tathāgata’s teaching—

They are not distinct; for they are without differentiation. Within the very nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness), the characteristics of the distinctions between matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are fully present.
How is this countered? It is said that all these aforementioned dharmas of merit are explained according to the two meanings of True Suchness (*tathatā*):
its aspect of permanence and its aspect of arising and ceasing. In both cases, there is no differentiation. Why? If explained according to the meaning of True Suchness, then it is one.
All phenomena are *tathatā*. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Although these various meanings of merit truly exist, they lack any marks of differentiation;
they are equal and of one flavor, being solely *tathatā*. This is spoken of from the perspective of the meaning of arising and ceasing."
Thus, the distinctions are shown based on the various manifestations of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

Although these distinctions are spoken of in relation to delusion, the characteristics of its virtues are without form; therefore, there are likewise no distinctions. Since it is explained according to these two meanings, both are without distinction.
How, then, could one say that within the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* there are the distinct characteristics of matter and mind? Thus, to cling to their existence—
The distinctions between matter and mind have vanished.

Fourth, one hears it stated in the sūtras that all worldly phenomena of birth, death, and defilement exist in dependence upon the tathāgatagarbha, and that all dharmas do not depart from true suchness (tathatā).
Because this is not understood, [people] claim that the tathāgatagarbha is its own intrinsic substance.
All phenomena of birth and death in the world are possessed [by sentient beings]. How are they to be remedied?

Because the *tathāgatagarbha* has, from the very beginning, possessed only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which are not separate from, not severed from, and not different from the meaning of *tathatā*;
whereas the defiled phenomena of afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges exist only as delusions, being by nature fundamentally non-existent from the start. From...
Since beginningless time, it has never been associated with the Tathāgatagarbha;
therefore, if the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha possessed deluded phenomena, it would be impossible for its realization to bring about the eternal cessation of delusion.
This refutes the view that clings to the existence of defilement by way of an inherent nature. Fourth, "Below" clarifies the conditions for the arising of such clinging.
This means hearing the sūtras state that all worldly phenomena of birth-and-death and defilement exist in dependence upon the *dharmatā* (nature) and do not depart from *tathatā* (suchness).

However, because one does not understand what the Tathāgata has taught—that true reality is without self-nature, that it becomes delusion according to conditions, and that this delusion is itself devoid of self-nature—it is entirely...
Because its essence is itself reality (*tathatā*), within this very nature of being the storehouse (*ālaya*) there exist all the defiled phenomena of worldly birth and death.

How are these to be countered? It is said that within the *tathāgatagarbha* there are only virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; because they accord with the true nature, they do not depart from suchness.
Conversely, the afflictions and defiled phenomena of birth and death, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, arise solely based upon ignorance. Only...

These are falsely existent; their nature is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning. Because they contradict the true nature, they have never been in accord with the *tathāgatagarbha* since time immemorial.

How could there be any defiled phenomena of birth and death within the nature? If there were false phenomena within the nature of the *garbha*, then those false phenomena would possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If they possessed an intrinsic nature, how could one then realize the principle and attain accord with it?
It is impossible for one who has permanently stilled delusions to hold such [a view]. In this way, the attachment to the view that the nature is subject to defilement is dispelled.
Fifth, one hears it stated in the *Sūtras* that because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is birth and death; because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, [there is nirvāṇa].
They attain *nirvāṇa*. Because they do not understand, they claim that sentient beings have a beginning;
because they perceive a beginning, they further claim that the *nirvāṇa* attained by the Tathāgata has an end, and that he returns to become a sentient being once again. How is this countered?

Because the *tathāgatagarbha* has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning. If one were to say that there are further sentient beings outside the three realms...
That which "begins its arising" is what is taught in the scriptures of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, because the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit (*aparānta*), and the nirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas corresponds to it, it likewise has no posterior limit.
This refutes the view of beginningless and endless arising and ceasing. Fifth, "Below" clarifies the conditions for the arising of attachment.

This means that upon hearing the sūtras state that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa exist in dependence upon the nature (dhātu), yet failing to understand that what the Tathāgata taught is that both the nature and saṃsāra are beginningless, and that both nirvāṇa and the nature are endless, one consequently clings to sentient beings.
There is the view of a beginning. Because they perceive a beginning, they further cling to the notion that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa has an end and that he returns to become a sentient being.

This arises from hearing the teaching that the false depends on the true, whereby they conclude that the true comes first and the false follows; thus, they give rise to the view of a beginning and an end.
How is this to be remedied? It is said that since birth and death exist in dependence upon the Tathāgatagarbha, and yet the Tathāgatagarbha...
There is no prior limit; thus, ignorance and saṃsāra likewise have no beginning.

To say that there is a first arising of sentient beings outside the three realms is the teaching of the non-Buddhist *Mahābhūta-sūtra*. How could such a statement exist within the True Teaching of the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, even nirvāṇa exists in dependence upon the tathāgatagarbha, yet the tathāgatagarbha has no [beginning].
As for the "subsequent limit," the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa likewise has no subsequent limit.
How could the nirvāṇa attained by the Tathāgata have an end, such that he would return to becoming a sentient being? Therefore, it was said previously:
"Not born at the prior limit, not extinguished at the subsequent limit. In this way, the views of beginning and end are stilled.
Regarding the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*): because the two vehicles possess dull faculties, the Tathāgata taught them only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Since that teaching was not ultimate, they perceived the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, fearing birth and death, they falsely grasped at nirvāṇa.
How is this to be remedied? By means of the five aggregates: since their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-arising, there is no cessation; they are originally in a state of nirvāṇa.
