Why? Because by practicing the various worldly dhyānas and samādhis, one relies on the view of self and frequently gives rise to attachment to their flavor.
Bound to the three realms and shared with non-Buddhists, if one is not protected by spiritual friends, one will give rise to the views of non-Buddhists;
therefore, one must cultivate the Samādhi of True Suchness before one can enter the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, those who diligently and single-mindedly practice and study this samādhi shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life.
What are these ten? First, they will always be protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Second, they will not be terrified by any māras, evil spirits, or ghosts. Third, they will not be [influenced] by the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths.
1. One is no longer deluded or disturbed by spirits and deities. 2. One remains far removed from slandering the profound Dharma, and heavy karmic obstacles gradually become thin and light.
3. One extinguishes all doubts and all evil thoughts and observations. 4. One’s faith in the realm of the Tathāgatas increases. 5.
One is free from sorrow and regret, remaining courageous and undaunted within the cycle of birth and death.
Eighth, his mind is gentle and supple; he abandons arrogance and is not troubled by others.

Ninth, although he has not yet attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), at all times and in all objective spheres, he is able to diminish his afflictions (*kleśa*) and takes no pleasure in the world.
Tenth, if he does attain *samādhi*, he is not startled or disturbed by external conditions or any sounds.

This clarifies the benefits obtained through the cultivation of *śamatha*. Regarding the statement that one who cultivates and studies *samādhi* is protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:

it means that this *samādhi* is the fundamental basis for the cultivation and realization of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, those who cultivate and study it are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is because they are able to realize that all phenomena are mind-only (*cittamātra*) and do not grasp [at them].
Being unattached, one is not deluded or disturbed by various māras, heterodox teachers, and the like. One is able to realize the profound principle and sever the mind of continuity;
thus, one does not slander the profound Dharma and thins out the karmic obstacles of offenses. Because of deep faith in *tathatā* (suchness), the mind is free from discrimination;
thus, one can sever all doubts and eliminate evil conceptualizations, while one's faith increases.
Furthermore, because he can penetrate the non-arising of all phenomena and his mind is free from sorrow and regret, he is courageous and undaunted amidst birth and death.
Because he realizes the equality of all phenomena and his mind is free from arrogance, he cannot be troubled by others.
Being free from all defiled attachments and not clinging to worldly pleasures, he is able to diminish his afflictions; taking no delight in the mundane world, he enters deeply into samādhi.
Because one does not pursue worldly conditions, one is not startled or disturbed by external circumstances.
Furthermore, if a person practices only *śamatha*, the mind will become sunken, or laziness will arise, and one will take no delight in various virtues.

Being far removed from great compassion, one therefore cultivates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). One who cultivates contemplation should observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world cannot endure for long;
they undergo transformation and decay in an instant. All mental activities arise and perish from moment to moment; it is for this reason that there is suffering.
One should contemplate that all dharmas previously thought of were as fleeting as a dream; one should contemplate those currently being thought of...
All phenomena are like flashes of lightning; one should contemplate all phenomena that arise in the future as being like clouds that suddenly appear.
One should contemplate all embodied beings in the world as entirely impure, defiled by various stains, and not a single one of them worthy of delight.

This passage points out the faults of practicing [only one side] and exhorts the cultivation of the four contemplations. Generally speaking, the two dharmas of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) must be cultivated together.

If one cultivates only *śamatha*, there is a danger that the mind will sink into dullness and become indolent regarding the two benefits [of self and others]; therefore, one is exhorted to cultivate *vipaśyanā*.
As stated below in the section on "Cultivation," one is led to contemplate conditioned phenomena as impermanent; thus it says: "Conditioned dharmas cannot remain for long. One must...

It changes and decays in an instant. [The phrase] "all that is inferior" causes one to contemplate that the mind is suffering; therefore, it is said that it arises and ceases in every thought-moment. For this reason, it is suffering.

One should contemplate [the phrase] "that which is inferior," causing one to contemplate all phenomena contemplated throughout the three periods of time as being like a dream, like lightning, and also like clouds—ultimately all empty.
One should contemplate that having a body is entirely impure, such that not a single thing is worth delighting in. Thus one acts.
Having completed this contemplation, the mind naturally does not sink into despondency; rather, one practices various virtues and initiates activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

In this way, one should reflect that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have had their minds subject to arising and ceasing due to being permeated by ignorance, thereby undergoing all manner of great physical and mental suffering. Even now, they are beset by immeasurable afflictions.
Oppressed by this, the suffering of the future is likewise without limit; it is difficult to abandon and difficult to escape, yet sentient beings remain unaware of it.
Such beings are truly to be pitied. Reflecting thus, one should immediately and courageously establish a great vow:
"May my mind be free from discrimination, so that I may cultivate all virtuous merits throughout the ten directions until the end of time."
Come! By means of immeasurable skillful means, rescue and deliver all sentient beings suffering from affliction, causing them to attain the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa.

Because you have given rise to such a vow, at all times and in all places, regarding all wholesome deeds, you shall practice and study according to your capacity without abandoning them, with a mind free from indolence, except when seated in meditation, during which time you shall focus single-mindedly on *śamatha*. If...
All else should be thoroughly examined as to what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

This exhortation to contemplate the suffering of things is intended to inspire compassionate vows for the cultivation of all virtues. Thus, the following section restates the instruction to contemplate the suffering of things;
that is to say, once one has already contemplated impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity, one should furthermore reflect upon sentient beings.
Born as that which is perfumed by beginningless ignorance, the mind undergoes arising and ceasing; thus, one undergoes all manner of great suffering.
Yet, although sentient beings have endured immeasurable and boundless suffering throughout the three periods of time, they remain unaware of it—this is truly pitiable.
Therefore, one should give rise to vast vows to rescue and deliver them. [The vow says: "May I..."

"Regarding the mind free from conceptual discrimination": this causes the arousal of the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*), which is the non-perverted mind. "Pervading the lower [realms]" and so forth:

this causes the arousal of the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*), which is the vast mind. "Until the end of the future" and so forth: this causes the arousal of the compassionate mind (*karuṇācitta*), which is the long-term mind.

To cause [the mind] to descend, one immediately arouses the first thought. By "arousing it to descend," one restates the aforementioned great vow and concludes with an exhortation to diligent practice.

Therefore, it says: "Except when sitting, when one focuses exclusively on *śamatha* (calm abiding), at all other times—whether walking or standing—one should always observe what ought to be done and what ought not to be done."
Whether walking, standing, lying down, or rising, one should always practice the union of śamatha and vipaśyanā. That is to say:

although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen, one simultaneously contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed.
Although one contemplates the karmic retributions of good and evil through causes and conditions, one also simultaneously contemplates that their nature is ungraspable.
If one cultivates *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the mundane world and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles.
If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their inferior state of mind;

it also distances one from the ordinary person’s failure to cultivate roots of goodness. For this reason, these gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* mutually assist and complete one another, never being separated.
If one lacks both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one will be unable to enter the path to bodhi.

This is an exhortation to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* perfectly according to the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*). From "If walking" (*yadī gacchan*) below, the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is indicated by means of the four dignified postures.
What follows from "So-called" (*yathoktam*) below explains the characteristic of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together; for since one observes while in the state of calm abiding, although...

One contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn; yet, because one simultaneously contemplates that the harmony of causes and conditions ensures that karmic fruits are never lost, one extensively cultivates all manner of virtues to gather and transform sentient beings.
This is cultivation without cultivation, for it is through the very act of contemplation that one abides in cessation.

Thus, although one contemplates the convergence of conditions and extensively cultivates myriad virtues, this does not hinder the simultaneous disappearance of both subject and object, such that the two benefits—self and others—are perfected in equal measure.
"Exhausted. "Cultivating that which is not cultivated" explains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in terms of cultivation. The section beginning with "If one cultivates...
explains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in terms of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*). This is because ordinary beings, failing to realize that all phenomena are unborn, greedily cling to the world;
while those of the Two Vehicles, failing to understand non-arising, are timid and fearful of birth and death. Therefore, what is now shown is the very essence of contemplation.

"Stopping" (*śamatha*) causes ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who practice it not to become attached to the world, and causes those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who practice it not to be cowed by birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, it is said that it serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the ordinary being’s dwelling in attachment to the world and enables one to abandon the timid and inferior views of the Two Vehicles.

As for "if one practices contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) below, this likewise remedies two faults; namely, it remedies the inferior and weak mind of the Two Vehicles and causes one to contemplate universally.

Sentient beings give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This also cures the habit of indolence in ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), causing them to contemplate impermanence (*anityatā*) and other such truths to spur the cultivation of wholesome practices.

Therefore, it is said that [this practice] serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) for failing to give rise to great compassion, and to ordinary persons for remaining distant from the cultivation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

From "By this" onwards, the preceding points are restated to establish their mutual correspondence; by means of this, both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are able to act as antidotes.

Because the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are all subject to faults, one knows that *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) mutually assist and complete one another, rather than being separated or abandoned.
This is because, when *śamatha* assists *vipaśyanā*, and *vipaśyanā* does not depart from *śamatha*, one does not dwell in saṃsāra.
When *vipaśyanā* assists *śamatha*, and *śamatha* does not depart from *vipaśyanā*, one does not dwell in nirvāṇa. Thus, as *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practiced together, one dwells in neither.
If one [understands] birth-and-death and nirvana [in this way], then one can ultimately realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Conversely, if one lacks both calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), then one will be unable to enter the path to bodhi.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds may become timid and weak.
Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings;
thus, they dread that the faculty of faith will be difficult to perfect and intend to retreat. You should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to gather in and protect such faith.

That is to say, by means of the causal conditions of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains birth in a buddha-land of another direction according to one’s vow, constantly beholds the Buddha, and is forever separated from the evil realms. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly mindfully recollects Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated with the vow to seek birth in that world, they shall immediately attain birth there. Constantly...

Because they have seen the Buddha, they shall never regress. If they contemplate that Buddha’s true suchness-dharmakāya and constantly and diligently practice it, they will ultimately attain birth there, for they abide in right concentration.

This refers to the occasion of cowardice and retreat; it is presented to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded recollection. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Next" clarifies the intention behind cowardice and retreat.

The section beginning with "One should know" indicates and points to the skillful means of protection and guidance. The section beginning with "As in the Sūtra" cites the scripture to establish the proof.

If one observes the lower [stages], this is stated to manifest the superiority of focused mindfulness. Regarding the phrase "for those who are beginners in these dharmas," this refers to the five preceding categories of dharma;
because practicing these five gates can accomplish the four kinds of faith, it says, "desiring to seek correct faith.
Regarding the phrase "their minds are timid and weak," this means that sentient beings have newly given rise to awakening within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Delusive karma has accumulated since beginningless time, whereas virtuous conduct is only now being cultivated and studied.

With the environment being powerful and the mind weak, and the obstacles being heavy while the power [of the mind] is slight, one must focus on cultivating the mind; how could one not feel fear? Moreover, in this Sahā world, one does not constantly encounter a Buddha.
Since one does not encounter a Buddha, how can the Dharma be heard? Under such circumstances, the wheel of suffering is easily turned, while right faith is difficult to attain.

[This is] established. It is because they intend to regress. For the sake of such individuals, the Tathāgata employs the skillful means of focused mindfulness to gather and protect them, causing them to focus their minds on the Buddha.
Thus, according to their vows, they attain birth in the buddha-fields of other directions and are forever separated from the evil realms.
Once born in those buddha-fields, they constantly encounter the Buddhas; therefore, they never again suffer regression. This is the tenth [point].

"Faith is non-retrogression. Regarding the passage "If one contemplates the lower [stages]": this means that whereas previously there was only single-minded mindfulness, here it includes contemplation of principle (*li*).

Since contemplation of principle is superior to the previous single-minded mindfulness, one should cultivate it with diligence; thus, one will ultimately attain birth [in the Pure Land], abide in right concentration, and enter the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) of non-retrogression.
This concludes the text of the *zhengzong* (the main teaching). What follows is the section on circulation (*liutongfen*).
The section on the practice of faith has already been explained. Next, the section on the benefits of encouraging its practice will be explained.
Thus, I have provided a general exposition of this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the profound realm of the Tathāgata, to remain free from slander, and to enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and cultivate it thoroughly.

One will ultimately attain the unsurpassed Way. If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, it should be known that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.
Even if someone were able to transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm, causing them to practice the ten wholesome paths, it would not equal the merit of a person who, for a single meal—
Recently, I have been reflecting precisely upon this Dharma; its merit surpasses that of the former [teachings] beyond all comparison.
Furthermore, if a person receives, upholds, contemplates, and practices this treatise for even a single day and night, the resulting merit will be immeasurable, boundless, and impossible to describe.
Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to [expound it] for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas...
One could not exhaustively praise his meritorious virtues. Why is this? Because the virtues of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) are inexhaustible;
the virtues of this person are likewise thus, without limit or boundary.

This serves as an incentive for those who are indolent and fail to advance; it raises further benefits to encourage cultivation. The first two phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce what follows.
"In this way" and below recapitulate the previous discussion. "If there be" and below generally reveal the benefits of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Indeed, the principles elucidated in this treatise—such as the one mind, the two gates, and the three greatnesses—are the profound realizations attained by all Buddhas.
Because this is the ultimate sphere of realization, those who wish to maintain right faith, avoid slander, and reach the unsurpassed path should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it.
If a person—[the following section] separately reveals the benefits of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

That is to say, the principles elucidated in this treatise are the very foundation upon which all Buddhas attain enlightenment; therefore, one who hears them without fear shall succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas. Thus, for the sake of all...

This is the Buddha’s prophecy. To illustrate this, let us set aside the merit of the transformed person (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) and separately manifest the benefit of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

That is to say, while the good deeds performed by the transformed person are mundane wholesome roots (*sāsrava-kuśala*), reflecting upon the Dharma for even the duration of a meal is a cause for the supramundane (*anāsrava*).
Thus, the virtue of reflecting on the Dharma far exceeds the merit of the transformed person; it is so great that it cannot be compared to it.
Furthermore, the section beginning with "Next, below" separately reveals the benefits of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

This means that although one may cultivate based on this treatise for only a single day and night, because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), its merit is boundless and immeasurable; how could it ever be fully described?

For this reason, even though all Buddhas were to praise it for immeasurable and incalculable eons, they would still be unable to exhaust it. The section beginning with "Why is this? explains why they cannot exhaust it through praise.
This is because the merit of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inexhaustible, and thus the merit of its cultivation is likewise boundless;
therefore, it cannot be fully extolled.
Any sentient beings who, within this treatise, disparage it or fail to believe in it, shall receive the retribution for their transgressions for immeasurable eons (*kalpa*).
They will experience great suffering and distress. Therefore, sentient beings should simply rely on faith;
they should not slander it, for to do so would deeply harm themselves and others, severing the seeds of the Three Jewels.
This is because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying upon this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-wisdom by practicing according to it. One should know this.
Bodhisattvas of the past have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma; bodhisattvas of the present are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma;
and bodhisattvas of the future shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma.
Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study it.
This passage cites the offense of slandering and disparaging [the Dharma] in order to conclude with an exhortation to believe and practice. The phrase "Those who...

and so forth cites the suffering resulting from the offense of lack of faith, exhorting belief and warning against slander. The phrase "Because all... and so forth explains the reason why the Three Jewels would be severed.
Indeed, that which this treatise elucidates is the lineage of the Three Jewels and the *dharmakāya* of sentient beings; it is upon this that all Buddhas rely to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on this to enter the Buddha-wisdom, to slander, revile, or disbelieve it is to sever the lineage of the Triple Gem and to destroy the Buddha’s nirvana.
This not only harms oneself but also harms others; therefore, the retribution for such offenses will cause one to undergo great suffering and distress for immeasurable kalpas.
"One should know" and below concludes the exhortation to believe and practice, referring to the three periods of time.
Since Bodhisattvas have all attained pure faith by relying upon this Dharma, sentient beings likewise should practice and study in accordance with it.
The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in summary according to the *dhāraṇī*.
"Dedicate this merit in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā) for the universal benefit of the entire realm of sentient beings.
This is the concluding summary of the dedication. The first two lines summarize what has been explained;
that is to say, this brief treatise follows the profound and vast meaning taught by the Tathāgata, condensing it into a few words. Therefore...
"Profound and great meaning" refers to the general summary of the preceding [sections]. The final two lines dedicate the merit of composing this treatise toward all sentient beings.

This is because Bodhisattvas originally act for the sake of sentient beings—removing their doubts, abandoning their attachments, giving rise to Mahāyāna faith, and enabling them to leave suffering behind and attain happiness—and it was for this purpose that he composed this treatise.
Therefore, upon its completion, he immediately dedicates the merit of composing the treatise [to others].
It is of the same dharma-nature and extends universally toward all sentient beings, causing those who see it or hear it to each believe,
understand, and practice, thereby entering the samādhi of *tathatā* and attaining ultimate, remainderless *nirvāṇa*.

Formerly, Master Mìzàng Kāi first established the site for the carving of the Tripitaka at Qingliáng Miaodé.
I once stayed there with my staff, and while I was lecturing on this treatise and its commentary with two or three fellow practitioners of the Dharma, Master Kāi also participated therein.

Whenever they reached obscure or difficult passages, the Master would pose challenging questions and engage in debate with the assembly of students, investigating and elucidating the points in great detail.
As soon as the lecture was concluded, the Master addressed me, saying: "This treatise is concise in its phrasing yet profound in its principles."

This is truly the crux of all Mahāyāna sūtras. However, the division of the text and analysis of its meaning are overly detailed, and since the commentaries and records do not harmonize, I fear that those who peruse it will find it difficult to achieve a unified understanding. You are capable of eliminating the superfluous and adopting the concise.
"I shall synthesize the *Shuji* (Commentary) and compile it in the manner of the *Lengyan Zuanyu* (Annotated Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).
Is this not most fortunate? I immediately replied, "This is a noble undertaking. However, I am ashamed that my talent and insight are dim and short-sighted, and my literary skills are unrefined.

Were I not to exert myself in this task, I would surely fail to honor your elegant intention. How could I allow myself to neglect such a compilation? Not long after, the project for the Tripitaka carving began.

The Master moved south to Shuangjing, and I too took up residence there. During the intervals between my meditation and recitation, I would immerse my spirit in this scripture, investigating it repeatedly until I had largely grasped its essential points.
Consequently, I divided the chapters and explained the meanings, recording the essentials while pruning away the redundancies.
I synthesized the various treatises and harmonized the commentaries and records. After three years, through both winter and summer, the draft of my commentary was finally completed. It was not...
I have ventured to carve this woodblock for circulation, intending it as a personal resource for my own study. Just then, Master Baoshi Yun and Xiaoruo Ma saw it and were delighted in their hearts;
they generously contributed funds with the desire to publish it through printing.

Because I admire the sincerity of both the monastics and the laity in their devotion to the Dharma, I have accordingly authorized its publication so that it may be corrected and refined by those throughout the various quarters.
